subject to the admissibility precondition Γ t : Admissible (T). Collapse requires an admissibility certificate. A term whose type is not Admissible (·) cannot be collapsed—this is a hard type error, not a runtime exception. Unlike the earlier presentation of this operator as bare “observation,” Collapse here is the committed act of adopting a task-relative quotient as constraining for later computation; the pure act of looking that produces o in the first place is not itself an event and is treated separately in Section [sec:view-vs-collapse].

nodes.title: VIEW versus COLLAPSE
nodes.heading: section
text: The decisive repair this edition makes is to separate pure observation from committed Collapse. A definition of Collapse as “observation under a rule” conflates two operations that later chapters—particularly the operational semantics and the Rust implementation—already treat differently in practice: a pure query that returns a value without touching history, and a committed event that appends to history. Making this explicit here prevents the equivocation from propagating into the minimality argument, the transition semantics, and the categorical treatment.
Definition (View: Pure Projection). The view of history H_t under observation c is
[equation]
VIEW does not append an event, does not change operational state, and does not consume possibility. Looking is not a world transition:
[equation]
Definition (Attest). An attestation is a tuple
[equation]

where o = c(H_t), ρ records provenance (who or what produced the observation and by what mechanism), and states the task or constraint for which the observation is being admitted. An attestation is a precondition for Collapse, not itself an event on H.
Definition (Collapse as Committed Quotient Adoption).
[equation]

VIEW is not a fifth primitive operator, because it is a meta-level query rather than an event-producing transformation; it never appears on the left-hand side of a world transition. Collapse remains a primitive because adopting a quotient as constraining is irreducible to Pop, Refuse, or Bind: none of those three records that a projection's result has been accepted as a boundary on later computation. The four-operator calculus is therefore preserved, with VIEW sitting outside it as the pure function every Collapse presupposes.

nodes.title: Why These Four and No Others
nodes.heading: section
text: The minimality of the four operators follows from an analysis of what operations on possibility space are conceptually irreducible.

Pop is irreducible because commitment—the foreclosure of alternative futures—cannot be expressed as a combination of documentation, dependency recording, or observation. It is the primitive act of narrowing possibility.

Refuse is irreducible because documented inadmissibility is distinct from commitment: it records that a path was considered and found inadmissible, which is information that commitment cannot record. A commit of the alternative does not document why the refused path was refused. Reasons are evidence that survives collapse; without them, refusal is indistinguishable from non-consideration.

Bind is irreducible because dependency recording—coupling two trajectory elements—cannot be expressed as commitment or refusal. A bind creates a relationship between elements without consuming either; no combination of Pop and Refuse produces this effect.

Collapse is irreducible because observation under a specific rule is distinct from all three of the above. Pop, Refuse, and Bind all operate on the history and option space; Collapse maps from history space to observable state space under a specified projection. It is the meta-operation that makes histories visible.

Proposition (Representation Adequacy of the Four Operators). The four operators {P_x, R_x,r, B_a,b, C_x,c,o,ρ,} suffice to encode the following constructs: variable assignment, conditional branching, function application, exception handling, memory deallocation, and concurrent event recording.

Remark (Why this is a proposition, not a theorem). This statement is downgraded here from “theorem” to a representation claim. Exhibiting encodings for six constructs demonstrates representation adequacy for those constructs; it does not establish general completeness over an arbitrary source language. A genuine completeness theorem would need to fix a source calculus L, a compositional translation - : L → Spherepop, and an operational correspondence theorem relating reduction in L to reduction of the translated term in Spherepop. No such calculus or correspondence theorem is given in this manuscript; “Completeness of the Four Operators” should therefore be read as a research proposition motivating future work, not as an established result.
Proof of representation adequacy. We establish expressibility for each construct.
Variable assignment x := v: Express as P_v followed by B_x,v. The commitment records the value choice; the bind records the name-value dependency.
Conditional branch on predicate φ: Express as P_φ^+ if φ holds, or R_φ^+,ConstraintViolation(φ) followed by P_φ^- if not. The refusal records why the positive branch was not taken.
Function application f(a): Expressed as LamIntro(x) followed by Apply(a)—a deferred Pop. The closure freezes the option space at the moment of abstraction; application is the moment of commitment.
Exception throwing: Expressed as R_t, r (documented inadmissibility without system destruction). The type Refused (T, r) carries the reason as a first-class certificate.

Memory deallocation: Expressed as R_p, Deallocated where p is the pointer symbol. The refusal records that the memory region is no longer admissible to access, making use-after-free a type-level error.

Concurrent event recording: Expressed via Meld, the monoidal composition of two histories. Two concurrent worlds (H_1, Ω_1) and (H_2, Ω_2) are combined as (H_1 ++ H_2, Ω_1 Ω_2) under an appropriate ordering convention.

nodes.title: A Genuine Completeness Result: Boolean Circuits
nodes.heading: section
text: The remark above named exactly what a real completeness theorem would need: a fixed source calculus, a compositional translation into Spherepop, and a correspondence theorem showing the translation is faithful. For one restricted but well-understood source calculus—Boolean circuits—all three are available, and the result below is a genuine theorem rather than a representation claim. It does not close the general completeness question left open above (an arbitrary imperative or functional language is not a Boolean circuit), but it is real, provable progress on a well-defined fragment, and it doubles as a clean illustration of the VIEW/Collapse distinction from Section [sec:view-vs-collapse] in a setting small enough to check by hand.
Definition (Boolean Interpretation of the Four Operators). Fix the two-element domain {0, 1} and define a map - _B from Spherepop's primitives to Boolean operations:
[equation]

where eval_B recursively evaluates a term built from P, R, B under this interpretation. Under this reading, Pop supplies a committed Boolean input; Refuse realizes complement; Bind realizes conjunction; and Collapse projects the resulting judgment—a VIEW in the sense of Section [sec:view-vs-collapse], not yet a commitment. The judgment becomes a committed Collapse event only once it is attested: eval_B(e) is a pure read of what the circuit currently evaluates to, and Attest( - _B, eval_B(e), ρ, ) is what would make adopting that Boolean judgment as binding an actual Collapse event, exactly as in the general case.

Definition (Boolean Circuit Calculus L_Bool). Fix L_Bool to be the calculus of Boolean circuits over a finite set of Boolean-valued inputs, built from and with arbitrary fan-out (i.e., a shared input may feed multiple gates). This is source calculus enough for the theorem below; the translation - : L_Bool → Spherepop sends a circuit built from and to the corresponding term built from R and B, with each circuit input realized by a Pop and the circuit's output read by Collapse under the interpretation of Definition [def:boolean-interpretation].

Theorem (Boolean Completeness of Refuse and Bind). Every Boolean function f : {0,1}^n → {0,1} is expressible as C(t) for some Spherepop term t built only from P, R, and B (no use of Collapse except at the outermost position).

Proof. This is the translation of a classical fact—{, } is a functionally complete basis for Boolean logic—through -. Every Boolean function has a disjunctive normal form, a disjunction of conjunctions of literals; is eliminable in favor of and via De Morgan's law, $x y = ( x y), so every Boolean function is expressible using only$ applied to the input variables. Each input variable is realized by a Pop; each becomes an R; each becomes a B; the whole expression is read by a single outer C. This is exactly - applied to the DNF circuit for f, which lies in L_Bool.

Gate & Construction & Formula Buffer & A → P → C → Y & C(P(A)) = A Not & A → R → C → Y & C(R(A)) = A And & A, B → B → C → Y & C(B(A,B)) = A B Nand & A, B → B → R → C → Y & C(R(B(A,B))) = (A B) Nor & A, B → R, R → B → C → Y & C(B(R(A),R(B))) = (A B) Or & A, B → R, R → B → R → C → Y & C(R(B(R(A),R(B)))) = A B Canonical gate constructions from P, R, B, C. Nor needs no final negation because A B = (A B) already, by De Morgan; Or is Nor negated once more.

Remark (Xor and Xnor, and a correction to an earlier informal diagram). An informal circuit diagram developed alongside this manuscript rendered Xor and Xnor with a typeset formula carrying one stray closing parenthesis—an artifact of how it was generated, not a conceptual error, since the diagrammed gate-level wiring (two Nots feeding a two-stage And/Or lattice) is a standard, correct realization. The cleanly parenthesized forms, verified against the truth table below, are
[equation]
[equation]

obtained by realizing A ⊕ B = (A B) ( A B) and its negation directly as nested Or/Nand-style compositions of the constructions above. As with any Boolean function, other gate-count-minimal realizations of Xor and Xnor exist; Theorem [thm:boolean-completeness] guarantees expressibility, not a unique or minimal circuit.

Remark (What this does and does not settle). Theorem [thm:boolean-completeness] is a genuine completeness theorem for L_Bool: the source calculus, the translation, and the correspondence (DNF expressibility, then a literal term-for-gate substitution) are all fully specified, unlike the six-construct representation-adequacy claim above. It does not, by itself, upgrade that broader claim to a theorem: Boolean circuits are combinational and have no notion of sequencing, admissibility, or refusal-with-reasons, so this result says nothing about whether an arbitrary program in some fixed imperative or functional source language translates faithfully into Spherepop. What it does establish is that the concern behind Proposition [thm:completeness]—that six worked examples might not generalize—does not apply uniformly: for at least one natural and non-trivial fragment, the four operators (in fact, only two of them) are provably complete, not merely adequate for the cases checked.

nodes.title: The Conservation Law
nodes.heading: section
text: The four operators satisfy a conservation law that reflects the fundamental structure of possibility.
Theorem (Conservation of Possibility). For any legal execution sequence
[equation]

where each step is one of P_x, R_x,r, B_a,b, or C_x,c: |H_t| is strictly monotonically increasing: |H_t+1| = |H_t| + 1. |Ω_t| is monotonically non-increasing. Under pure Pop dynamics, |H_t| + |Ω_t| = |Ω_0| for all t.
Proof. (i) Every operator appends exactly one event to H, so |H_t+1| = |H_t| + 1.
(ii) P_x removes x from Ω; the remaining operators do not modify Ω. Hence |Ω_t+1| ≤ |Ω_t|.

(iii) Under pure Pop dynamics, every step removes exactly one element from Ω and appends one event to H. Starting from |H_0| = 0 and |Ω_0|, after t steps |H_t| = t and |Ω_t| = |Ω_0| - t, giving |H_t| + |Ω_t| = |Ω_0|.

The conservation law has the structure of a physical conservation principle: possibility is not created or destroyed—it is either consumed (by Pop) or documented as inadmissible (by Refuse). The operators Bind and Collapse record relationships and observations without affecting the possibility budget.

Definition (Selection-Budget Invariant). Define the event weight function w : E → N by w(Pop (x)) = 1, w(Refuse (x,r)) = 0, w(Bind (a,b)) = 0, w(Collapse (x,c,o,ρ,)) = 0. For a world (H, Ω), the selection-budget invariant is
[equation]
This quantity was originally called the “generalised possibility functional,” but that name overstates what it measures; see the remark below.
Theorem (Conservation of the Selection-Budget Invariant). For any legal execution sequence, Π(H_t, Ω_t) = |Ω_0| for all t.

Proof. At each step, exactly one of four operators is applied. Pop: |Ω| decreases by 1; w(Pop ) = 1 is added. Net change: (-1) + 1 = 0. Refuse, Bind, Collapse: |Ω| unchanged; w = 0 is added. Net change: 0. In every case Π(H_t+1, Ω_t+1) = Π(H_t, Ω_t).

Remark (Π does not measure reachable possibility). Because Refuse and Collapse can constrain admissibility, A (H), without changing Ω (Section [sec:admissibility-set] below), Π is conserved trivially by construction and does not track total reachable possibility: a history full of refusals that narrow A (H) down to a single admissible symbol has the same Π as one with no refusals at all, even though the two differ enormously in what remains reachable. Π should therefore be read as a bookkeeping identity over $(Pop -consumption) + (remaining options)$, not as a general reachability measure. A separate admissible-continuation functional, defined over A (H) rather than Ω alone, would be needed to track reachability properly; none is developed in this manuscript. The committed Collapse event, in particular, can narrow task-relative admissibility even when |Ω| is unchanged, precisely because it commits the world to treating a quotient as constraining—this is invisible to Π by construction, not because Collapse has no effect.
Corollary (Irreversibility of Execution). For any non-empty execution sequence, |H_t+1| > |H_t|. Therefore no legal execution can return to a previous world state (H_t, Ω_t).
Proof. Every operator appends exactly one event to H, so |H_t+1| = |H_t| + 1 > |H_t|. Since H grows strictly, (H_t+1, Ω_t+1) ≠ (H_t, Ω_t).

This irreversibility is not a limitation but a feature. It is the formal correlate of the phenomenological observation that histories are primary: a world that could return to a prior state would be a world in which the history of the intervening steps was undone, which is not computation but its negation.

nodes.title: Histories as the Primary Objects
nodes.heading: section
text: Before introducing types, evaluators, or compilers, we must characterize the mathematical structure of the objects that are primary in the Spherepop ontology. Histories are not merely lists of events. They form a category, and the category structure constrains what operations on histories are meaningful.
Definition (History). A history over event alphabet E is a finite sequence H = [e_1, e_2, , e_n] with each e_i ∈ E. The empty history is ε = [].
Definition (History Concatenation). For histories H_1 = [e_1, , e_m] and H_2 = [f_1, , f_n],
[equation]
Proposition (History Monoid). The triple (H , ++, ε) is the free monoid over E.

Proof. Associativity of ++ follows from list concatenation associativity. ε is the left and right identity. Freeness: every history H is uniquely determined by its event sequence, and no non-trivial relation among generators holds.

nodes.title: The History Category
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (History Category Hist). Define the category Hist as follows: Objects: option spaces Ω ⊆ Ω_0. Morphisms: Hom(Ω, Ω') is the set of histories H such that starting from Ω, executing H yields Ω'. Composition: H_2 H_1 = H_1 ++ H_2 (execute H_1 first, then H_2). Identity: id_Ω = ε.
Proposition (Hist is a Well-Defined Category). Hist satisfies all category axioms.
Proof. Associativity of composition follows from associativity of ++. ε is the identity morphism since $H ++ = H = ++ H$.

Proposition (Hist is a Free Strict Monoidal Category). (Hist , ++, ε, ) is a free strict monoidal category where the tensor product H_1 H_2 is the Meld operation (parallel composition of histories) and the monoidal unit is the empty option space with empty history.

Remark. The free monoid structure forces append (extend by one generator) and meld (monoidal composition of two histories) as the only legitimate history operations. The absence of remove and undo is the mechanization of freeness: there are no relations among generators. pub fn append(&mut self, event: Event) self.events.push(event); // one generator pub fn meld(&mut self, other: &History) self.events.extend(other.events.iter().cloned()); History equality H_1 = H_2 is the primary criterion of program identity.

nodes.title: Unique Factorisation
nodes.heading: section
text: Theorem (Unique History Factorisation). Every non-empty history H = [e_1, e_2, , e_n] admits a unique factorisation into primitive generators:
[equation]
No other factorisation into generators exists.

Proof. Since H is the free monoid over E, every element has a unique normal form as a sequence of generators. The generators are singletons [e]; freeness of the monoid guarantees there are no non-trivial relations among generators.

Remark. Unique factorisation is what makes history equivalence a decidable correctness criterion for compilation. If two execution paths produce the same history, they must have produced the same sequence of primitive events in the same order.

nodes.title: Admissibility as a Set-Valued Function
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Admissible Futures). For a history H, the set of admissible future symbols is
[equation]
Definition (Admissibility Contraction). Let H' = H ++ [Refuse (x, r)]. Then A (H') ⊆ A (H), and specifically x A (H') while x may have been in A (H).

Remark. The asymmetry between Pop and Refuse is critical. Pop contracts the structural option space Ω. Refuse contracts the admissibility set A (H) without touching Ω. Two execution paths may have the same Ω while having different A (H)—they are structurally equivalent but semantically distinguished by their refusal histories. This distinction is invisible to any state-centric computational model.

nodes.title: Big-Step Semantics
nodes.heading: section
text: The big-step relation t, W v, W' relates terms and worlds to values and resulting worlds.

Definition (Evaluation Result). An evaluation result is a triple (v, H, a) where v is a value, H is the accumulated history, and a ∈ {, } is the admissibility flag. The admissibility flag is if every operation in H was admissible and if any refusal was encountered.
The key invariant is that evaluation never discards history. Every step appends to H; no step modifies or removes prior events. The world grows monotonically.
pub struct EvalResult pub value: Value, pub world: World, // world.history grows monotonically pub admissible: bool,

nodes.title: Multi-Step Reduction
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Multi-Step Reduction). The multi-step reduction →^* is the reflexive transitive closure of →. A term t is normal if there is no t' with t → t'.
Theorem (History Monotonicity). If (H_0, Ω_0) →^* (H_n, Ω_n) then H_0 is a prefix of H_n: there exists H' such that H_n = H_0 ++ H'.
Proof. By induction on the length of the reduction sequence. Each step appends exactly one event to the history. The result follows by transitivity.
Theorem (Option Space Monotonicity). If (H_0, Ω_0) →^* (H_n, Ω_n) then Ω_n ⊆ Ω_0.
Proof. Only Pop removes elements from Ω; all other operators leave it unchanged. By induction, Ω can only shrink.

nodes.title: The Insufficiency of Unparameterized Collapse
nodes.heading: section
text: The original Spherepop design represented collapse as simply Collapse(Symbol). This was insufficient, and the insufficiency is philosophically illuminating.

Observable state depends on how you look. The same history, examined by different observers with different observational frameworks, yields different observable states. A collapse without a rule is a collapse into an unspecified notion of visibility. The rule is not an implementation detail; it is what makes the observation meaningful.
Definition (Collapse Rule). A collapse rule is a function c : H → O_c from the history monoid to an observational space O_c.
Definition (Observational Equivalence). Two histories H_1, H_2 ∈ H are observationally equivalent under rule c, written H_1 _c H_2, if and only if c(H_1) = c(H_2).

Three distinct objects are gathered under the informal phrase “observable state,” and it is worth separating them explicitly, since the manuscript's earlier presentation moved between them without comment:
the attainable observation values, O_c = im(c); the equivalence class of a history, [H]_c ∈ H / _c; the actual observation, o = c(H), a single element of O_c.

Definition (Observable State as Quotient). Strictly, O_c need not literally equal H / _c as a set; it is canonically isomorphic to the quotient once c is treated as surjective onto its own image (which it always is, tautologically, once O_c is taken to be im(c) rather than some a priori larger codomain):
[equation]
Under this identification, an observable state may be treated interchangeably as an equivalence class of histories or as the value c(H) that names it.

Observable state is not a state. Observable state is a quotient. Two histories that are globally distinct may be observationally indistinguishable under a specific collapse rule. This is a feature: the collapse rule specifies which distinctions are relevant to a given question.

nodes.title: The Four Canonical Rules
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Identity Rule). c_I : H → H is the identity: c_I(H) = H. Under the identity rule, every event is visible and O_I H.
Definition (LastWrite Rule). c_LW maps H to the most recent pop for each symbol, with subsequent refusals retroactively removing symbols:
[equation]
Definition (Accumulate Rule). c_acc(H) maps each symbol to the count of its Pop events:
[equation]
Definition (Projection Rule). For a label prefix L, the projection rule π_L restricts to events whose symbol names share prefix L:
[equation]

Proposition (Coarsening Order). The collapse rules form a partial order by coarsening: c_1 ≤ c_2 iff _c_2 ⊆ _c_1 (finer equivalence = more informative observation). Under this order: c_I is the finest; π_L is coarser than c_I; c_LW and c_acc are incomparable in general.

nodes.title: The Collapse Functor
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Observable-State Category Obs _c). For a collapse rule c, define the category Obs _c: Objects: observable states o ∈ O_c. Morphisms: Hom(o_1, o_2) is the set of observable transitions transforming o_1 into o_2 under rule c. Composition: sequential observable transition.
Definition (Collapse Functor). For collapse rule c, define F_c : Hist → Obs _c by F_c(Ω) = c(ε_Ω) on objects and F_c(H) = c(H) on morphisms.
Theorem (Functoriality of Collapse). F_c is a well-defined functor when c respects composition:
[equation]
Proof. Identity preservation: F_c(ε) = c(ε) = id_O_c. Composition preservation: $F_c(H_2 H_1) = F_c(H_1 ++ H_2) = c(H_1 ++ H_2) = c(H_2) c(H_1) = F_c(H_2) F_c(H_1)$ when c respects composition.

Remark. The functoriality of collapse elevates it from an implementation detail to a category-theoretic object. Collapse is a structure-preserving map between categories. The collapse rule specifies which structures are preserved, and different rules preserve different structures. c_LW is not generally functorial because the last-write of a concatenated history is not the composition of the last-writes of its parts—a later segment can retroactively affect the observable state of an earlier one.

Remark (Scope of the functoriality claim). It bears restating explicitly that Theorem 1.101 (Functoriality of Collapse) is conditional: an arbitrary observation function c : H → O_c does not automatically induce a functor. Functoriality holds precisely when c is a monoid homomorphism, c(H_2 ++ H_1) = c(H_2) c(H_1), and fails otherwise, as the c_LW example immediately above shows. “Collapse Functor Functoriality,” entered in the theorem status table as proved, should be read as proved for composition-respecting collapse rules, not as a general statement about all observation functions. A more ambitious construction—a quotient category built from a congruence on histories, requiring H_1 _c H_1' and H_2 _c H_2' to imply H_1 H_2 _c H_1' H_2'—is not attempted here and remains open.

nodes.title: The Universal Property of Collapse
nodes.heading: section
text: Theorem (Universal Property of Collapse). Let q_c : H → O_c be the quotient map for rule c. If f : H → X is any function satisfying
[equation]
then there exists a unique f : O_c → X such that f = f q_c.

Proof. By the universal property of quotient sets. Define f([H]_c) = f(H). This is well-defined because f is constant on equivalence classes. Uniqueness: any f satisfying f = f q_c must map [H]_c to f(H).

Remark. The universal property says that observable state is not one representation among many. It is the universal representation among all representations that identify the same histories as c does. Every coarser observation necessarily passes through O_c.

nodes.title: The Inadequacy of Value-Set Types
nodes.heading: section
text: The standard interpretation of types—a type is a set of admissible values—is adequate for state-centric languages. It is insufficient for Spherepop.

Consider what a type must certify in a history-primary setting. A value v of type T is not merely a member of a set. It is the result of a path through history that reached v without violating any constraint represented by T. The type is not a description of v at a moment; it is a certificate about the history that produced v.

nodes.title: The Type Language
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Spherepop Types). The type language of Spherepop is defined inductively:
[equation]
The simple function type T_1 → T_2 is notation for Π(_ : T_1).T_2.

The distinctive types carry certificates, not just values: Admissible (T): the path that produced this term was admissible. Refused (T, r): the term was encountered but found inadmissible for reason r. The reason is part of the type—two terms refused for different reasons have genuinely different types. Collapsed (T, c): an admissible term was observed under collapse rule c and the observation is sealed. The rule c is part of the type.

nodes.title: The Type Rules
nodes.heading: section
text: We write Γ t : T for the standard typing judgement.
[equation]
Pop transforms any typed term into an admissible term. It is the mechanism by which structural commitment produces a reachability certificate.
[equation]
Refusal is typed: the type carries the reason. A term refused for ConstraintViolation(c) has a type formally distinct from one refused for NotAvailable.
[equation]
Collapse requires an admissibility certificate. A term whose type is not Admissible (·) cannot be collapsed—this is a hard type error, not a runtime exception.

[equation]

nodes.title: Open Worlds and Closed Worlds
nodes.heading: section
text: During implementation of the Spherepop type checker, a conflict emerged between how the interpreter and type checker treated free variables. The apparent bug conceals a genuine theoretical discovery: which behavior is correct depends on which assumption about the boundary of the world is in force.
Definition (Closed-World Context). A closed-world context Γ_c satisfies:
[equation]
The absence of a declaration is the absence of the object.
[equation]
Definition (Open-World Context). An open-world context Γ_o satisfies:
[equation]
The absence of a declaration is undecided possibility.
[equation]
Proposition (Monotonicity of Provability). $_c _o Provable(_c) Provable(_o)$.

Remark. The open/closed world distinction is not an engineering convenience. It is the mechanization of an epistemological commitment: a closed-world type checker assumes complete knowledge of the reachable; an open-world type checker assumes partial knowledge. A language whose fundamental ontology is about possibility space cannot leave this distinction implicit. The TypeMode is preserved through extend: a closed-world context cannot silently become open-world mid-derivation.

nodes.title: Principal Theorems
nodes.heading: section
text: Theorem (Collapse Soundness). If Γ collapse(t, c) : T then Γ t : Admissible (T') for some T', and T = Collapsed (T', c).
Proof. By inversion on [T-COLLAPSE]: the only rule that derives a Collapse judgement requires the premise Γ t : Admissible (T), so the inner term must have an admissible type.
Theorem (Type Preservation). If Γ t : T and t → t', then Γ t' : T.

Proof. By structural induction on the reduction relation →. The key cases are [T-POP], [T-REFUSE], and [T-COLLAPSE], each mapping a reduction step to an admissibility transformation closed under the respective rule. Beta-reduction requires a substitution lemma: Γ, x : T_1 b : T_2 and Γ a : T_1 implies Γ b[x := a] : T_2[x := a].
Theorem (Progress). If t : T (well-typed in the empty context) then either t is a value, or there exists t' such that t → t'.

Proof. By structural induction on t. Variable terms are values. Lambda terms are values (closures). pop, refuse, bind, and collapse of a well-typed inner term either reduce (if the inner term reduces) or produce a value (if the inner term is a value).

nodes.title: Dependent Process Types
nodes.heading: section
text: The current Process (T_1 T_2) is first-order. A dependent process type allows the output type to depend on the specific value consumed.
Definition (Dependent Process Type). A dependent process type
[equation]
allows the type of the output process to depend on the value x of the input. This is the natural extension of dependent type theory into the process calculus setting.
Example. A function that reads a file and returns a proof that the file was read can be typed as:
[equation]
The Admissible in the output type certifies that the reading path was admissible—no access violation occurred, the file existed, and the permissions were valid.

nodes.title: Admissibility Lattices
nodes.heading: section
text: The current admissibility structure is Boolean: a term is admissible or not. A more refined theory recognizes that admissibility is graded.

Definition (Admissibility Lattice). An admissibility lattice (L, ≤, , , , ) is a bounded lattice where: is full admissibility: the trajectory satisfies all constraints. is total inadmissibility: the trajectory violates all constraints. _1 _2 is the admissibility under the conjunction of constraints c_1 and c_2. _1 _2 is the admissibility under the disjunction.
Definition (Graded Admissibility Type). Admissible _(T) denotes admissibility at level ∈ L. The standard Admissible (T) is Admissible _(T).
Proposition (Admissibility Lattice Typing). The typing rule for graded admissibility is:
[equation]
Collapse requires admissibility at level at least _0 for some threshold _0 determined by the collapse rule c.

Remark. Admissibility lattices connect the Spherepop type theory to the admissibility geometry program of the RSVP and CLIO frameworks. The xylomorphic criterion λ < 1 from the admissibility field is a threshold condition in a continuous admissibility lattice, where admissibility is measured by a scalar λ and collapse is only valid when λ falls below the threshold.

nodes.title: Proof-Carrying Refusal
nodes.heading: section
text: The RefusalReason type is currently a vocabulary for inadmissibility. It is not yet a proof system. A fully realized Spherepop type system would require RefusalReason to be a proof term: evidence that can be checked, not merely a label.

Definition (Proof-Carrying Refusal). A proof-carrying refusal is a refusal of the form refuse(t, π) where π is a proof term of type Inadmissible(t, Ω)—a formal certificate that t is inadmissible given the current admissibility set A (H).
Definition (Inadmissibility Proof System). The inadmissibility propositions and their proofs are:
[equation]
Each proposition has a type-theoretic proof term, and refuse(t, π) is only well-typed when π proves one of these propositions for t.

Theorem (Refusal Completeness). Every inadmissible trajectory has a proof-carrying refusal at some point. That is, if A (H) x for some x that is later attempted, then there exists a proof term π of Inadmissible(x, A (H)).
Proof. x A (H) implies r. Refuse (x, r) ∈ H. The proof term π = AlreadyRefused(x) witnesses that x is in the refused set, which is defined as the complement of A (H).

nodes.title: The Seven Note Classes as Operator Realizations
nodes.heading: chapter
text: The four Spherepop operators—Pop, Refuse, Bind, Collapse—are abstract operations on possibility space. Notes are their physical realization in cognition, computation, language, and civilization. This chapter develops the correspondence systematically.

nodes.title: The Classification Principle
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Dominant Operator). The dominant operator of a note class is the Spherepop operator that accounts for the primary function of notes in that class. Most notes mix operators, but each class has a dominant one.

Theorem (Notes as Spherepop Programs). Every note is a Spherepop program. Every Spherepop program is a note. The correspondence is given by the following bijection between note classes and operator combinations: Note Class & Dominant Operator & Secondary Operators Capture & Refuse & — Prospective & Bind & Pop (deferred) Repair & Refuse + Pop & — Coordination & Bind & Refuse Refusal & Refuse & — (pure form) Generative & Pop & Bind Collapse & Collapse & —

nodes.title: Capture Notes
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Definition (Capture Note). A capture note is a note whose primary function is to preserve a continuation that exists at the time of note creation but is expected to become inaccessible. In Spherepop terms, a capture note performs a Refuse operation with respect to the projection σ : H → S: it preserves history fibers that the projection would collapse.

A photograph refuses the collapse of a perceptual trajectory. An audio recording refuses the collapse of a sonic trajectory. A laboratory notebook refuses the collapse of a procedural and cognitive trajectory.

Proposition (Capture Notes and Refuse). A capture note N performs a Refuse operation with respect to the projection σ : H → S if and only if there exists a history fiber h ∈ σ^-1(S) such that P_A(c_h, t | N) > P_A(c_h, t), where c_h is the continuation associated with history h.

The quality criterion for a capture note is not fidelity to the original state but adequacy as a reconstruction substrate. A photograph that captures the correct person but not the context may be a poor capture note even at high resolution, if the lost context is what matters for future reconstruction. The adequacy of a capture note depends on what future continuations are anticipated.

nodes.title: Prospective Notes
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Definition (Prospective Note). A prospective note is a note whose primary function is to preserve access to a continuation that does not yet exist at note creation time but is anticipated. In Spherepop terms, a prospective note performs a Bind operation between present agent state A_t and future continuation c_t'.

A calendar entry binds future action to present scheduling. A blueprint binds future construction to present design. A roadmap binds future development to present strategic commitment. Source code binds future computation to present specification—and is unique in that the binding is mechanically executable.
Proposition (Prospective Notes and Temporal Binding). A prospective note N performs a Bind operation if and only if
[equation]
where t' > t and the conditioning on A_t indicates the agent's present state is available in both cases.
Proposition (Collective Reachability from Coordination). Let A_1, , A_n be agents with independent continuation spaces C _1, , C _n. A coordination note N increases collective reachability if
[equation]
The proposition captures the supraadditive character of coordination: bound agents can traverse paths that no individual could reach alone.

nodes.title: Repair Notes
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Repair Note). A repair note is a note whose primary function is to reduce the cost of reconstructing a continuation after it has been or is anticipated to be interrupted. It combines Refuse (preserving the history of the trajectory against collapse) and Pop (enabling re-entry at a specific point after interruption).

Theorem (Notes as Pre-emptive Repair). Every note N with positive repair value R_v(N, c) = C_r(c) - C_r(c | N) > 0 constitutes a pre-emptive repair: it reduces expected reconstruction cost prior to any failure occurring.

Proof. R_v(N, c) > 0 implies C_r(c | N) < C_r(c). Since the note exists before any failure occurs, the cost reduction is in force from the moment of note creation. The note therefore functions as a repair mechanism that precedes the event it repairs for.

A troubleshooting guide is a repair note: a stored Pop operator for a class of failure states. Each entry says: if you arrive at this failure state, the continuation from here to a functional state runs through these steps.

nodes.title: Refusal Notes
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Refusal Note). A refusal note is a note whose primary function is to prevent the collapse of an existing distinction, independently of whether the preserved distinction is expected to be used. It is the closest realization of the pure Refuse operation.
Mathematical proofs, cryptographic checksums, archival copies, legal records, and formal specifications belong to this class.
Proposition (Proofs as Refusal Notes). A mathematical proof P of theorem T from premises Γ satisfies
[equation]
for any agent A with sufficient background knowledge, at any future time t.

The proof refuses the collapse of an inferential trajectory into mere assertion. Its value is not actualized use but preserved potential: it maintains the reachability of the derivation whether or not anyone consults it.

nodes.title: Generative Notes
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Generative Note). A generative note is a note that creates access to continuations that were not reachable before the note's creation. It is the primary realization of the Pop operation: it opens new trajectories in possibility space.
Proposition (Generative Notes and Novel Reachability). A generative note N satisfies
[equation]
That is, N creates access to continuations that were previously unreachable.

Scientific theories, maps, programming languages, mathematical formalisms, and ontologies are generative notes. A programming language is a generative note that is mechanically executable: it defines not just a space of possible programs but a machine for traversing that space.

nodes.title: Collapse Notes and the Ephemerality Inversion
nodes.heading: chapter

nodes.title: The Hidden Class
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Collapse Note). A collapse note is an artifact that performs a deliberate projection σ_N : H → S_N, compressing a history or artifact into a more compact representation at the cost of detail, in order to make the representation navigable. It is the realization of the Collapse operator.

File names, titles, abstracts, indexes, summaries, taxonomies, classifications, labels, and keywords are all collapse notes. The paradox of collapse notes is that they appear to be the opposite of notes—they destroy information—yet they are indispensable to the function of every other note class.

Theorem (Necessity of Collapse Notes). For any sufficiently large collection of notes N, there exists a threshold |N | > K above which the reachability of individual notes in N decreases in the absence of collapse notes over N.

Proof. Search cost through an unstructured collection grows at least linearly with collection size. For |N | > K, exhaustive search becomes too expensive for practical use. A collapse note—index, catalogue, taxonomy—reduces search cost by imposing structure, making individual notes reachable at sublinear cost. Without such structure, notes become inaccessible through navigational failure, not destruction.

Remark. A word is a collapse note: it compresses a complex of experience, association, inference, and usage into a single retrievable token. A noun is a collapse note about a process. The passive theory would not recognize these as notes at all. The Spherepop theory recognizes them immediately as the most pervasive and powerful class of collapse notes civilization has developed.

nodes.title: The Ephemerality Inversion
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Continuation Completion). A continuation c is complete with respect to note N at time t if the trajectory encoded by N has been successfully traversed.

Theorem (Ephemerality Inversion). Let N be a note encoding a single continuation c. If c has been completed, then the destruction of N does not reduce the reachability of any remaining continuation. Therefore the ephemerality of N after completion of c implies neither loss nor failure.

Proof. By assumption, c is the sole continuation for which N increases reachability. After completion of c, V_C(N) = 0. Since continuation volume is zero, the destruction of N reduces reachability by zero.
The grocery list discarded at the supermarket exit has not failed. It has succeeded completely. The theorem generates an inversion of the passive theory's ranking:

Fate & Passive Theory & Continuation Theory Executed and discarded & Low value & Optimal Preserved and re-entered & Medium value & Valuable Preserved, never re-entered & High value & Unrealized potential

The celebrated survivors of antiquity—incomplete manuscripts, undelivered letters, abandoned plans—survive precisely because their continuations were never completed. The completed notes, the sent letters, the finished buildings, left no trace because they succeeded.

nodes.title: The Event IR and Compiler Correctness
nodes.heading: chapter
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction

nodes.title: The Failure of Traditional Compiler Correctness
nodes.heading: section
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction
text: The standard notion of compiler correctness is: a compiler is correct if the compiled program produces the same output as the interpreted program for every input. This criterion is adequate for state-centric languages. It is insufficient for Spherepop.
Two programs that produce the same final value may have constructed radically different histories to get there, and those histories are part of what the program is.

Definition (History Equivalence as Correctness). Let I : P → H be the interpreter function mapping programs to histories, and V : IR → H the VM mapping event-IR blocks to histories, and C : P → IR the compiler. A compiler C is correct if for all programs p and initial worlds W:
[equation]
Output equivalence (same final value) is a strictly weaker criterion that is insufficient for Spherepop.

nodes.title: Event IR
nodes.heading: section
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction
text: Conventional intermediate representations encode instructions that mutate machine state. Spherepop IR encodes events—records of occurrences that persist as part of the history the VM is constructing.
Definition (Event IR). The Spherepop intermediate representation is a sequence of IrEvent terms:
[equation]
Each event carries its reason or rule as a first-class argument, preserving the full certificate structure of the source term.
pub enum IrEvent Pop, Refuse reason: RefusalReason , Collapse rule: CollapseRule , Bind, Load(Symbol), Apply, LamIntro(Symbol, Type),

Proposition (IR Faithfulness). The compilation function C : Term → IR is faithful: for every primitive term t, C(t) contains exactly the event variants that I(t) would append to the history, with identical arguments.
Theorem (Replay Equivalence). The Spherepop compiler satisfies history equivalence for all programs expressible in the Spherepop core calculus.

Proof. By structural induction on program terms. For each primitive operation (Refuse, Bind, Collapse, Pop), the compiler emits the corresponding IrEvent variant, and the VM step performs exactly the same World mutation as the interpreter's eval case. The history appended is therefore identical. For Seq: each sub-term is compiled in order, and since histories compose by concatenation, the composed history of the compiled form equals that of the interpreted form by induction.
Theorem (Compiler Full Faithfulness).
[equation]
Proof. () By Replay Equivalence applied twice. () Similarly. The biconditional follows from the symmetry of history equivalence.
Corollary (Operational-State Faithfulness, Repaired). Under the same hypothesis,
[equation]

and likewise for the compiled/VM histories, so equal histories under Compiler Full Faithfulness entail equal operational states M_t (Section [sec:layered-world-model]) on both the interpreter and VM sides. This closes the gap the implementation chapter's replay test targets: the assertion world.materialized == fold_operational(&world.history) is exactly the case p_1 = p_2 of this corollary applied to a single program compared against its own operational-state cache.
Proof. F_op(-; M_0) is a function of H alone (Definition of Operational State, Section [sec:layered-world-model]); applying an equal function to equal arguments gives equal results.

Remark (History equality remains strictly stronger). The converse of Corollary [cor:op-state-faithfulness] fails in general: equal operational states do not entail equal histories. Two different, non-replay-equivalent event sequences can fold to the same operational-state cache—for instance, two orderings of Refuse events for distinct symbols produce the same admissibility index A (H) even though the histories differ as sequences, since A depends only on the set of refused symbols (Definition of Admissible Futures, Section [sec:admissibility-set]), not their order. Compiler correctness should therefore compare both criteria—history equality via Compiler Full Faithfulness, and operational-state equality via Corollary [cor:op-state-faithfulness]—with history equality understood as the strictly stronger of the two, exactly as the implementation chapter's revision requires.

nodes.title: Garbage Collection as Admissibility-Guided Collapse
nodes.heading: chapter
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction

nodes.title: The Standard Problem
nodes.heading: section
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction
text: In conventional languages, garbage collection identifies and reclaims memory that is no longer reachable from the program's roots. The criterion is purely structural: an object is garbage if no live reference points to it.

In Spherepop, the analogous question is: which portions of the history are no longer needed to support any reachable continuation? The answer is richer because it depends not just on structural reachability but on admissibility.

nodes.title: History Segments and Liveness
nodes.heading: section
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction
text: Definition (History Segment Liveness). A history segment H[i:j] = [e_i, e_i+1, , e_j] is live at time t if there exists an agent A and a continuation c such that: c is reachable at time t: P_A(c, t) > 0, and c depends on H[i:j]: P_A(c, t | H[i:j]) < P_A(c, t). A segment is dead if it is not live.

Definition (Admissibility-Guided GC). Admissibility-guided garbage collection removes dead history segments while preserving the admissibility certificates needed for future collapses. Formally, let A _live(H) be the set of future continuations still reachable. GC produces H' ⊆ H (as a subsequence) satisfying:
[equation]

nodes.title: GC as Collapse
nodes.heading: section
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction
text: Theorem (GC as Collapse Composition). Admissibility-guided GC is equivalent to applying a collapse rule c_GC that maps H to the subsequence of live events:
[equation]
c_GC is a valid collapse rule when liveness is stable under extension: if e is live in H, it is live in H ++ H' for all H'.

Proof. Liveness is defined in terms of reachable continuations. Since histories grow monotonically and Pop operations only add to the committed history, a past commitment that enables a reachable continuation remains enabling under history extension. Therefore c_GC respects composition: the GC of a concatenated history equals the concatenation of the GC of the parts.
Corollary (GC Preserves Admissibility). If c_GC(H) = H', then A (H') A _live(H).

Proof. GC removes only dead events. A dead Refuse event is one that marks a symbol x as inadmissible when x is no longer needed by any reachable continuation. Removing it restores x to the admissibility set. Since no live continuation needs x, this does not affect any future collapse certificate.

nodes.title: Three GC Strategies
nodes.heading: section
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction
text: Different collapse rules for GC yield different strategies with different cost-benefit profiles.

Definition (Mark-Scan GC). Mark-Scan GC applies the identity rule c_I to the subhistory of live events: it retains the full sequence of live events in order. This is the most informative strategy and preserves all historical structure needed for replay.

Definition (Quotient GC). Quotient GC applies a coarser rule c_LW to the history before collecting: it retains only the last commitment to each symbol. This is equivalent to state-based GC with a history log and loses intermediate state information.

Definition (Certificate-Only GC). Certificate-Only GC retains only Refuse events (inadmissibility certificates) and Collapse events (observation certificates), discarding all Pop and Bind events whose certificates have been sealed. This minimizes memory use while preserving the admissibility structure needed for future type checking.
Theorem (GC Strategy Tradeoff). Let M(c_GC) denote memory usage and R(c_GC) denote recovery power (the set of continuations that can be reconstructed after GC). Then:
[equation]

Proof. The identity rule retains the most events and therefore uses the most memory but also preserves the most recovery information. Each coarsening reduces both memory usage and recovery power by identifying more history segments as equivalent.

nodes.title: Admissibility Certificates and GC Safety
nodes.heading: section
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction
text: A key constraint on GC in Spherepop is that it must not invalidate pending type judgements. If a collapse term collapse(t, c) is waiting on the admissibility certificate Γ t : Admissible (T), GC must retain the history events that support that certificate.

Definition (GC Safety). A GC operation is safe if for every pending collapse judgement Γ collapse(t, c) : Collapsed (T, c), the history events needed to support Γ t : Admissible (T) are retained after GC.
Theorem (Safety of Certificate-Only GC). Certificate-Only GC is safe: it retains all Refuse events that contribute to any pending admissibility certificate.

Proof. The admissibility type Admissible (T) is established by the sequence of Pop and Refuse events that produced t. Certificate-Only GC retains all Refuse events (inadmissibility certificates) unconditionally. The Pop events can be inferred from the Collapse certificates that seal their results. Therefore all information needed for pending collapse judgements is preserved.

nodes.title: Error Correction as Certified Refusal
nodes.heading: chapter
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction

nodes.title: The Standard Approach and Its Limits
nodes.heading: section
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction
text: In conventional languages, error handling is an afterthought: exceptions are thrown when something goes wrong, and error handling code is written separately from the main computation. This approach has three problems. First, it treats errors as exceptional when they are often structurally inevitable. Second, it provides no information about why the error occurred. Third, it makes error recovery expensive because the history of the computation is not available.

In Spherepop, errors are not exceptional. Every Refuse event is a documented non-traversal of a possible path. Error handling is not separate from the main computation; it is part of the computation's history.

nodes.title: Error Correction Codes in History Space
nodes.heading: section
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction
text: Definition (History Redundancy). A history H has redundancy factor k if there exist k disjoint subsequences H_1, , H_k ⊆ H (as event subsequences) such that each H_i alone is sufficient to reconstruct the full admissibility certificate for the terminal collapse:
[equation]

Definition (Erasure-Correcting History). An erasure-correcting history with parameters (n, k) encodes k independent certificate paths through n events, such that any k of the n events are sufficient to recover the full admissibility structure.

Theorem (Error Correction via Redundant Refusal). If a history H with redundancy factor k ≥ 2 has m < k/2 events corrupted or erased, the correct admissibility structure can be recovered from the remaining events.
Proof. With redundancy k and fewer than k/2 erasures, at least k - k/2 > k/2 redundant paths remain intact. Majority vote over the surviving paths recovers the correct admissibility judgement.

nodes.title: Typed Error Propagation
nodes.heading: section
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction
text: Definition (Error Type). An error type is a type of the form Refused (T, r) where r is a proof-carrying reason. Error types carry the evidence of inadmissibility as first-class type-level information.
Definition (Error Propagation Rule).
[equation]
The handler b may produce a value of T_2 or propagate a refusal. The propagated refusal carries the original reason r, preserving the full provenance chain.
Theorem (Error Preservation). If Γ t : Refused (T, r) and there is no handler in scope for r, then r propagates to the nearest enclosing context that can handle Refused (·, r).

Proof. By the typing rules, Refused (T, r) types only propagate upward through [T-HANDLE] if the handler does not fully resolve them. Since every unresolved Refused (T, r) in a well-typed program must eventually reach a handler or become the return type of the program, propagation terminates at the program boundary with a documented reason.

nodes.title: Recovery as Certified Continuation
nodes.heading: section
nodes.part: Compilation, Garbage Collection, and Error Correction
text: Definition (Recovery Certificate). A recovery certificate for an error Refused (T, r) at world state W is a term recover : Refused (T, r) → Admissible (T') that transforms a documented inadmissibility into an admissible continuation of type T'.

Theorem (Soundness of Recovery). If recover : Refused (T, r) → Admissible (T') is a recovery certificate and Γ t : Refused (T, r), then Γ recover(t) : Admissible (T'). Furthermore, the history of recover(t) contains the full provenance chain from the original refusal to the recovery, ensuring that the recovery is not a silent erasure of the error.

Proof. By application of the recovery function type and [T-POP] applied to the result. The history contains the original Refuse (x, r) event followed by the recovery events. No history erasure is possible since histories grow monotonically.

Remark. Recovery in Spherepop is the computational analogue of repair theory: it restores access to a continuation after documented inadmissibility, but unlike silent error suppression, it preserves the full record of what went wrong and how it was addressed. The recovery certificate is a note—specifically a Repair Note—in the formal sense of the note taxonomy.

nodes.title: The Reviewer's Challenge
nodes.heading: section
text: Spherepop does not abolish the state illusion. It makes the quotient explicit, parameterised, and reversible whenever the underlying history is retained.

A careful reader will notice a tension. The document claims to resolve the state illusion—the loss of historical information caused by projecting history to state. Yet every output of a Spherepop program is a collapse: a value derived by applying a rule to a history. The programmer observes the collapsed value, not the history. Is Spherepop not simply relocating the state illusion?

This chapter addresses that challenge. We prove the Finite Observation Non-injectivity Theorem, which shows the challenge follows from the specified cardinalities rather than from the nature of observation as such, and then distinguish precisely between state erasure (which Spherepop eliminates) and state illusion (which bounded observation cannot eliminate).

nodes.title: The Finite Observation Non-injectivity Theorem
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (History-Faithful Observation). An observation map φ : H → O is history-faithful if it is injective: φ(H_1) = φ(H_2) H_1 = H_2.

Theorem (Finite Observation Non-injectivity). Let O be any set with |O| < |H |. Then every observation map φ : H → O is non-injective: there exist distinct H_1 ≠ H_2 with φ(H_1) = φ(H_2). Consequently, no computational system whose observable space has strictly smaller cardinality than its history domain can directly verify the history it constructed from that observable alone.
Proof. Since H = _n ≥ 0 E^n is countably infinite and |O| < |H |, by the pigeonhole principle φ cannot be injective. Therefore there exist H_1 ≠ H_2 with φ(H_1) = φ(H_2).

Remark. The qualified conclusion, and no stronger one, follows: every observation whose codomain has lower cardinality than its history domain is non-injective, and every non-injective observation induces a nontrivial quotient. This does not license the universal claim that “every observation is a quotient”—the Identity observation c_I : H → H, introduced elsewhere in this book, is injective by construction and induces the trivial quotient. Theorem [thm:no-direct-observation] is a cardinality constraint on bounded observables, not a claim about observation as such.

Remark (Observational loss is not custodial loss). This chapter's result concerns observational loss: a lossy view need not erase anything if H remains available elsewhere. State illusion, in the sense of Definition [def:state-illusion] below, is inevitable under bounded views; state erasure is a separate, architectural choice about whether H itself is retained. Conflating the two would make the coming results about custody and provenance (developed further in the discussion of physical inscription and recoverability) look like restatements of a cardinality theorem, when they are in fact claims about a different failure mode entirely.

nodes.title: Erasure versus Illusion
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (State Erasure). A computational system suffers state erasure if it irrecoverably discards the history H after computing σ(H). After execution, H is unavailable and only σ(H) remains.

Definition (State Illusion). A computational system presents a state illusion to its programmers if they can only observe σ(H) and not H directly. By Theorem 7.1, some state illusion is unavoidable for any non-trivial observable space.

Proposition (What Spherepop Eliminates). Spherepop eliminates state erasure: the history H is retained in world.history and is available to any observer. Spherepop cannot and does not eliminate the state illusion: the programmer's primary observable is c(H), not H, so distinct histories that agree under c remain indistinguishable from the perspective of that observation.
The correct claim is therefore: Spherepop does not abolish the state illusion. It makes the quotient explicit, parameterised, and history-preserving.

nodes.title: Rule Refinement as Disambiguation
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Rule Refinement Order). Collapse rule c_1 is finer than c_2 (equivalently c_2 is coarser than c_1), written c_1 c_2, if c_2 factors through c_1:
[equation]

Factorization is used here rather than the equivalent but more error-prone definition via reversed inclusion of induced equivalence relations, since the latter is easy to state backward. The two are consistent: c_1 c_2 in the sense above implies H_1 _c_1 H_2 H_1 _c_2 H_2, because c_1(H_1) = c_1(H_2) gives $c_2(H_1) = f(c_1(H_1)) = f(c_1(H_2)) = c_2(H_2). The Identity rulec_Iis the finest rule (everyc$ factors as c = c c_I); the trivial rule c_ mapping all histories to a single point is the coarsest.

Proposition (Disambiguation by Refinement). Let H_1 _c H_2 (histories indistinguishable under rule c) and H_1 ≠ H_2. Then there exists a finer rule c' c such that c'(H_1) ≠ c'(H_2). In the limit, c_I always disambiguates since c_I(H) = H exactly.
Proof. Take c' = c_I: since H_1 ≠ H_2 and c_I(H) = H, we have c_I(H_1) = H_1 ≠ H_2 = c_I(H_2).

nodes.title: Category Theory as Engine
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Remark (Rechecking after the VIEW/Collapse separation). Every categorical claim in this chapter concerning “observation” was written before Section [sec:view-vs-collapse] separated pure VIEW from committed Collapse. The functors O_c and the adjunction below concern projection or quotienting—VIEW, in the vocabulary of that section—not the event that records the adoption of a quotient as constraining. Where a left-adjoint or reflection is claimed, it is a reflection onto the observable category Obs _c via the pure map c; it says nothing, by itself, about when an observation is attested or collapsed into history. This chapter should be read with that reattribution in mind throughout.

nodes.title: The History-Observation Adjunction
nodes.heading: section
text: Remark (A naming collision this repair must resolve first). Before restating the adjunction, one more inconsistency has to be named. The symbol Hist has been used for two incompatible categories in this book: the History Category of Chapter [ch:collapse-quotient] has option spaces Ω ⊆ Ω_0 as objects and histories as morphisms between them, whereas the History Construction Functor below treats G(t) as a single history, which only typechecks if the objects of the target category are histories. These are not the same category, and no functor can target both at once. The repair introduces a second, explicitly named category for histories-as-objects, rather than continuing to overload Hist.

Definition (Prefix Category of Histories). Hist _ is the category whose objects are histories H ∈ H and whose morphisms are given by the prefix order: there is a (unique) morphism H → H' iff H is a prefix of H', i.e. H' = H ++ K for some K ∈ H. Composition is transitivity of the prefix relation; the identity on H is the trivial extension by ε. Since the prefix relation on finite sequences is a genuine partial order (antisymmetric: H H' and H' H force H = H'), Hist _ is a thin category (a poset viewed as a category), distinct from the morphisms-are-histories category Hist used elsewhere.

Definition (History Construction Functor, Repaired). Let Terms be the category whose objects are Spherepop terms and whose morphisms are reduction sequences. Define G : Terms → Hist _ by G(t) = I(t).history on objects. On morphisms, a reduction sequence from t to t' is sent to the prefix morphism G(t) → G(t'); this is well-defined because interpretation only appends events along a reduction, so I(t).history is always a prefix of I(t').history) when t reduces to t'.

For the observation side, functoriality of c with respect to prefix order is not automatic—it is exactly as delicate as the composition-respecting property already required for the Collapse Functor (Theorem 1.101), and for the same reason: c_LW is sensitive to what comes later in a history, so extending a history can move its LastWrite value in either direction, not monotonically.
Definition (Prefix-Monotone Collapse Rule). A collapse rule c : H → O_c is prefix-monotone if there is a partial order _c on O_c such that H H' implies c(H) _c c(H').

Example. The Identity rule c_I is prefix-monotone with _c_I = itself. The Accumulate rule c_acc, which counts occurrences of each symbol, is prefix-monotone under the pointwise order on count vectors: appending events can only increase counts. The LastWrite rule c_LW is not prefix-monotone under any order, for the same reason it fails to respect concatenation in Theorem 1.101: appending a write to x can move c_LW(H) to an unrelated value, not one comparable to the old value under any fixed order.

Definition (Observation Functor, Repaired). For a prefix-monotone collapse rule c, define O_c : Hist _ → (O_c, _c) by O_c(H) = c(H). This is a functor between thin categories (i.e., a monotone map of posets) precisely by the definition of prefix-monotonicity.

The earlier “History-Observation Adjunction,” stated only for c_I, is now visibly degenerate once this machinery is in place: since c_I is the identity map, O_c_I is the identity functor on Hist _, and the claimed bijection Hist (G(t), H) Terms(t, G^-1(H)) reduces to the tautology that G(t) = H iff t reduces to some term with that exact history—which is simply Replay Equivalence restated, not a nontrivial adjunction. Calling it an adjunction overstated what the identity-rule case actually shows.

Theorem (Reflection for Prefix-Monotone Rules). Let c be a prefix-monotone collapse rule equipped with a section s_c : O_c → H satisfying c(s_c(o)) = o for all o (a chosen canonical representative history for each observable value). Suppose further that s_c is order-reflecting: H s_c(o) c(H) _c o for all H ∈ H and o ∈ O_c. Then O_c s_c: viewing s_c as a functor (O_c, _c) → Hist _, it is right adjoint to O_c, and s_c exhibits (O_c, _c) as a reflective subcategory of Hist _.

Proof. For thin categories, an adjunction is exactly a Galois connection: monotone maps F : P → Q and G : Q → P between posets satisfy F G iff F(p) ≤_Q q p ≤_P G(q) for all p, q. Here P = H (ordered by ), Q = O_c (ordered by _c), F = O_c, and G = s_c. The hypothesis that s_c is order-reflecting is precisely H s_c(o) c(H) _c o, which is the Galois-connection condition read in one direction; the other direction, O_c(H) _c o H s_c(o), is the same statement. Hence O_c s_c.

Example (The Accumulate rule satisfies the hypotheses). Let s_acc send a count vector o to the (essentially unique, up to event ordering within a symbol) history obtained by popping each symbol the number of times its count in o specifies, in some fixed canonical order (say, symbol index order). Then c_acc(s_acc(o)) = o by construction, and H s_acc(o) iff every count in H is ≤ the corresponding count in o (since s_acc(o) realizes exactly those counts and prefixes of it realize sub-counts in the canonical order), which is exactly c_acc(H) _acc o. So Theorem [thm:reflection-repaired] applies to c_acc, giving a genuine, nontrivial reflection: (O_acc, _acc) is a reflective subcategory of Hist _, with O_acc as the reflector.

Remark (What this repairs and what it does not). The theorem is stated for prefix-monotone rules with an order-reflecting section—hypotheses satisfied by c_I (trivially) and c_acc (shown above), but not by c_LW, matching its established failure to respect composition in Theorem 1.101. The original “Collapse as Reflection” claim, below in the derivations chapter, is restated to point back here rather than re-deriving a weaker or inconsistent version. As with the Functoriality theorem, this result concerns the pure functor O_c—VIEW, in the sense of Section [sec:view-vs-collapse]—and says nothing about when an observation is attested or committed as a Collapse event; the reflective subcategory is a fact about the geometry of quotienting, not about which observations a program has chosen to adopt as binding.

nodes.title: Collapse Rules Form a Lattice
nodes.heading: section
text: Proposition (Observational Lattice). The set of collapse rules ordered by refinement c_1 c_2 forms a complete lattice. The meet of {c_i} is the finest rule at least as fine as all; the join is the rule generated by the union of equivalence relations.

Proof. The meet and join are defined by the standard lattice operations on equivalence relations. Completeness follows because arbitrary intersections and generated equivalence relations of equivalence relations are again equivalence relations.

nodes.title: Sheaf-Theoretic Semantics
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Observational Site). Fix collapse rules {c_i} and observable states {o_i}. The observational site O is the category whose objects are observational regions {c_i^-1(o_i)} and whose morphisms are inclusions c_j^-1(o_j) c_i^-1(o_i) when the former is contained in the latter.
Proposition (H is a Sheaf). The history presheaf H on O—defined by H (U) = {H ∈ H : H ∈ U}—satisfies the sheaf condition: compatible local histories glue uniquely to global histories.
Proof. Compatibility means event sequences agree on their shared prefixes. Two compatible event sequences agreeing on all overlaps determine a unique concatenation.

Proposition (State Illusion as Non-Injectivity of Sections). A collapse rule c exhibits state illusion if and only if the observable sheaf O_c fails to determine a unique global section of H. There exist distinct H_1, H_2 ∈ H (H ) with the same section in O_c(H ).

The sheaf structure ties the local (what one observer sees under one rule) to the global (the full history that all rules project from). Sheaf cohomology measures the obstruction to lifting local observations to global histories—which is precisely the observational entropy.

nodes.title: CLIO Projections and Active Geodesic Inference
nodes.heading: chapter

nodes.title: Collapse Rules as CLIO Projections
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (CLIO Projection). A CLIO projection π : X → M maps a representation space X to a manifold M of observational strata. In the Spherepop setting: X = H (history space), M = O_c (observable state space under rule c), and π = F_c (the collapse functor).
Definition (Observational Entropy). For a collapse rule c and observable state o ∈ O_c, the observational entropy is
[equation]
Theorem (Entropy Monotonicity Under Rule Refinement). If c_1 c_2 (c_1 finer), then for every o ∈ O_c_1:
[equation]
Finer rules have smaller or equal fibre sizes.
Proof. Since c_1 c_2, every _c_1-class is contained in a _c_2-class. Therefore |c_1^-1(o)| ≤ |c_2^-1(c_2(H))| for any H ∈ c_1^-1(o).

Remark. Observational entropy S_c(o) = |c^-1(o)| is exactly the CLIO quantity S_π(m) = Vol(π^-1(m)) in the discrete Spherepop setting. Spherepop is a discrete computational instance of the CLIO projection program.

nodes.title: The Santoro–Waghmare–Panaretos Unification
nodes.heading: section
text: Theorem (Representation Changes Topology). Let ρ_1, ρ_2 : X → Y be two representation maps with τ_ρ_1 ≠ τ_ρ_2. Then there exist x_1, x_2 ∈ X such that x_1 _ρ_1 x_2 but x_1 _ρ_2 x_2, or vice versa. The two representations disagree on whether x_1 and x_2 are the same object.

Proof. If τ_ρ_1 ≠ τ_ρ_2, there exists an open set U ∈ τ_ρ_1 τ_ρ_2. Then U = ρ_1^-1(V) for some V ⊆ Y, but U ≠ ρ_2^-1(W) for any W. Therefore there exist x_1, x_2 with ρ_1(x_1) = ρ_1(x_2) but ρ_2(x_1) ≠ ρ_2(x_2).

Remark. This theorem is the general form of the observation that representations reorganise topology. It applies uniformly to: (1) the Santoro–Waghmare–Panaretos kernel embedding, which converts metrically close distributions into topologically singular Gaussian measures; and (2) Spherepop collapse rules, where refinement moves history pairs between equivalence classes.

In the kernel case, the topological change is forced by the Feldman–Hájek theorem. In the collapse case, the topological change is chosen: the programmer selects the rule, thereby choosing which distinctions are topologically visible. Both are instances of the same structural operation.

nodes.title: Active Geodesic Inference
nodes.heading: section
text: The Spherepop framework connects to a broader theory of intelligent systems as trajectory-maintaining structures.

Definition (Active Geodesic Inference). An intelligent system performs active geodesic inference if it actively shapes its configuration space through energetic and entropic constraints, forming low-action trajectories through possibility space rather than following predetermined state transitions.

Proposition (Spherepop as Active Geodesic Substrate). Spherepop's irreversible, scope-based semantics enforce history-sensitivity and prevent incoherent superposition by construction. Pop operations commit to specific trajectories; Refuse operations document inadmissible branches; the history preserves the full record of path selection. Spherepop is therefore a natural substrate for implementing active geodesic inference: the history is the geodesic; the admissibility set is the constraint field; collapse is the observation that seals a trajectory as complete.

Definition (Formal Intelligence). Intelligence is the capacity of a system to remain within a family of dynamically admissible, low-action histories by actively reshaping its configuration space's geometry. This definition extends across scales, encompassing learning within a lifetime, evolution across generations, and reasoning within an episode.

Theorem (Intelligence as Note Infrastructure). An intelligent system with formal intelligence in the above sense is necessarily a note-producing system: it constructs and maintains Capture, Prospective, and Repair notes as part of the mechanism by which it reshapes its configuration space. Notes are the mechanism by which intelligent systems install future reachability from present positions.

Proof. A system that maintains low-action histories across time must preserve information about its past trajectories (Capture Notes), commit to future trajectories (Prospective Notes), and recover from trajectory interruptions (Repair Notes). Each of these is a note class in the formal taxonomy. Therefore any formally intelligent system produces notes as a structural necessity, not a contingent feature.

nodes.title: Memory as Event Structure
nodes.heading: section
text: The MEM8 architecture treats memory not as isolated symbol storage but as structured pattern access where retrieval depends on preserving relationships, locality, and accessibility. Memory is not a database; it is a cognitive substrate whose operations are structurally similar to Spherepop's history operations.

Proposition (MEM8 as Spherepop Instance). The MEM8 architecture is a biological instance of the Spherepop framework: MEM8 Layer & Spherepop Note Class Episodic layer & Capture notes Procedural layer & Repair notes Semantic layer & Coordination notes Indexical layer & Collapse notes Theoretical layer & Generative notes

Remark. A notebook is a miniature MEM8. A Git repository is a miniature MEM8. An archive is a miniature MEM8. Each stores structured trajectories organized to make reconstruction possible. The difference between a good archive and a poor one is not quantity of material stored but quality of access structure: how well the collapse notes and coordination notes that organize the collection preserve the reachability of trajectories within it.

nodes.title: Repair as Pre-emptive Refusal
nodes.heading: section
text: Repair Theory holds that repair is the restoration of access to a trajectory that has been interrupted. The connection to Spherepop is not metaphorical but structural: repair is the execution of a Repair Note that was created in anticipation of the failure.

Theorem (Note Taxonomy as Failure Taxonomy). The seven note classes correspond bijectively to seven classes of anticipated trajectory failure: Note Class & Anticipated Failure Capture & Experiential collapse Prospective & Intention-execution gap Repair & Procedural interruption Coordination & Coordination failure Refusal & Distinction collapse Generative & Inferential poverty Collapse & Navigational failure

nodes.title: Civilizational Scale
nodes.heading: section
text: Definition (Civilizational Note Infrastructure). Let civilization Z possess note infrastructure N = {N_1, , N_k}. The collective reachability is
[equation]
where C (N_i) is the set of continuations preserved or enabled by N_i.
Theorem (Civilizational Collapse). The destruction of note infrastructure N decreases collective reachability even when underlying truths remain unchanged:
[equation]
A civilization that loses its note infrastructure does not become ignorant. It becomes unable to reach its own knowledge.

Proof. By definition, R(Z) includes all continuations preserved by elements of N. If N is destroyed, no element contributes to collective reachability. Since some continuations are accessible only through N, it follows that R(Z N ) < R(Z). The underlying facts are not destroyed, but the paths that made them accessible are.

Technology & Reachability Horizon & Dominant Note Classes Speech & Minutes to hours & Coordination, Capture Story & Decades & Capture, Generative Writing & Centuries & All classes Printing & Populations & Coordination, Refusal Digital storage & Replication & All classes, at scale Version control & Modification history & Repair, Capture Network & Distribution & Coordination, Generative

Each note technology expands the reachability horizon by addressing failure modes the preceding technology could not prevent. Writing prevents the death of witnesses. Printing prevents the destruction of individual copies. Version control prevents the loss of developmental history through modification. The history of civilization is the history of expanding note infrastructure.

nodes.title: From Observation to Reconstruction
nodes.heading: section
text: The preceding chapters established that every collapse rule c : H → O_c induces an observational entropy S_c(o) = |c^-1(o)|. This quantity measures the size of the fibre associated with an observation. A collapse with small observational entropy preserves many distinctions between histories. A collapse with large observational entropy identifies many histories and destroys information. The natural next question is not merely how many histories are hidden, but how difficult it is to reconstruct the correct one.
Definition (Reconstruction Cost). Let o ∈ O_c. The reconstruction cost of o is
[equation]
where C(H) denotes the computational effort required to identify history H from among the candidates in the fibre.
Definition (Uniform Reconstruction). A reconstruction procedure is uniform if every history in c^-1(o) is considered equiprobable given only the observation o.
Theorem (Entropy Lower Bound on Reconstruction). For any uniform reconstruction procedure,
[equation]
for some positive constant k depending only on the cost model C.

Proof. The fibre c^-1(o) contains N = |c^-1(o)| candidate histories. Any reconstruction procedure must distinguish among these alternatives.
