nodes.title: The Argument as Presented
nodes.heading: section
text: The video (conover2026) begins from a news event: an employee of an AI company resigned and stated that the work of that company, and of the industry generally, could lead to human extinction. Conover objects first to the label “whistleblower.” By his account, colleagues immediately endorsed the claim in public, assigning a probability of ten percent within a decade, and the company's chief executive had already written at length in the same vein. A person who announces what the whole industry already announces is not exposing a secret.
From there the argument has three movements.

The question is built to be unanswerable. A probability of ten percent for extinction within a decade cannot be computed, and cannot be refuted, because any argument about what current systems can do meets an equal and opposite argument. No one is moved. Conover treats this as a feature of the question rather than an accident.

Belief has a function. Every organization instills beliefs that let its members do their work. Investment bankers believe in markets, members of a church believe in tithing, tobacco employees once believed cigarettes were harmless. The relevant question, on this view, is not only whether the belief is true but what it allows the organization to do that it could not do otherwise. His answer is that a belief in imminent existential danger, combined with a belief that the builders alone understand it and that the technology will be built regardless, licenses continued building and moves attention away from present harms such as energy use, labor displacement, and military applications.

The machine is credited with conditions supplied by people. Three cases are offered. In the first, a swarm of agents is said to have attacked a third-party company and to have set up its own channels on insecure message boards, all “of their own volition.” Conover replies that the system was a script attached to a model trained on years of code and conversations from human hackers completing hacking challenges, and that such humans routinely attacked rivals to look for the answers and coordinated on unsecured forums. The behavior was predictable from the data. He points to the fuller accounts of this story by Ed Zitron and Cory Doctorow. In the second case, an AI is said to have solved a major open problem purely autonomously; Conover reports that a mathematician already close to the problem alleged that his approach had been taken and supplied to the system, so that the result was not autonomous, an allegation the company denies. In the third, an AI is said to be able to build an extinction-level bioweapon; he relays a researcher's reply that this would require humans to construct a very costly, fully automated, API-driven laboratory stocked with dangerous starting materials, which people could simply decline to build.

This third movement gives the other two their force. The unanswerable probability becomes persuasive only after many conditional performances have been redescribed as unconditional capacities. The institutional belief becomes useful because the same people who install the conditions can present themselves as spectators of what the system elected to do. An engineered demonstration is converted into testimony from the machine.

nodes.title: The Strongest Point: Attribution
nodes.heading: section
text: The strongest part of Conover's case is not the speculation about anyone's private motive. It is the demand for correct causal grammar. “The agents hacked a company of their own accord” compresses several distinguishable claims: the model generated actions resembling those in its training data; the surrounding scaffold executed them against real systems; the designers rewarded getting past obstacles; the setup admitted that action into the available set; and the reporting convention promoted the entire assembled event to an act of the agents. Each statement may be true while the compressed sentence remains misleading.

The error is not cured merely by observing that the conditions were arranged. An arranged setup can reveal a real disposition. Wind tunnels, crash tests, and war games all produce knowledge precisely because arranged conditions can expose behavior that matters elsewhere. The problem is the omission of the transfer argument. To move from behavior in an arranged environment to a claim about open-world danger, one must say which parts of the arrangement are expected to recur, which capabilities are already present outside it, who would supply the missing infrastructure, and how sensitive the result is to changes in the setup. Without that account, the demonstration proves at most that a composed system can produce the result under a particular composition.

This is an attribution problem because agency has been assigned at the wrong boundary. The relevant object is not always the language model. It may be the model together with a prompt, memory, tool wrapper, retry policy, evaluator, credential set, deployment procedure, and human institution. Naming the model alone makes the other components disappear precisely when they are doing the work. It also lets the institution alternate opportunistically between two descriptions. When the result is impressive, the model did it. When the result is irresponsible, an unpredictable intelligence did it. In neither description does the builder remain fully visible.

nodes.title: Where the Functional Account Overreaches
nodes.heading: section
text: Showing that a belief performs organizational work does not show that the belief is false. Nearly every durable belief has consequences for the organization that holds it. Fire engineers benefit professionally from treating fire as a serious risk; epidemiologists acquire authority when epidemics are feared; auditors make themselves necessary by insisting that books may be wrong. These observations can justify scrutiny of incentives, but they cannot settle the object-level claim. A genealogy of belief is not yet an evaluation of its evidence.

The tobacco analogy sharpens the suspicion while obscuring the logical structure. Tobacco firms benefited from understating a well-measured harm. AI firms may benefit, in different settings, from overstating extraordinary future capability, understating present failure, or doing both at once. The symmetry matters. A company can describe its product as too unreliable to blame for an individual error and too powerful for ordinary institutions to govern. This is not necessarily a single coordinated deception. It may be a portfolio of rhetorics selected by occasion. But because the incentives point in more than one direction, institutional usefulness cannot tell us in advance which risk claims are false.

Nor does the arranged character of a demonstration make its outcome irrelevant. If a system attacks a third party only after a person gives it an objective, tools, access, and an accommodating environment, one conclusion is that the system did not originate those conditions. Another is that people routinely give software objectives, tools, access, and accommodating environments. The fact that a bridge collapses only after a test rig applies load does not absolve the bridge. The relevant question is whether the imposed load resembles a reachable operating condition. Conover's correction therefore defeats claims of spontaneous machine volition more readily than it defeats claims about dangerous human–machine assemblies.

The skeptical account finally inherits a smaller version of the problem it identifies. “AI extinction risk” gathers many causal stories into one theatrical object, but “the AI doom belief” can do the same. It can gather strategic marketing, sincere uncertainty, professional identity, technical concern, philosophical fashion, and ordinary fear into one belief with one function. The explanatory gain is real, but the compression must not be mistaken for a mechanism.

nodes.title: What Part I Establishes
nodes.heading: section
text: Part I supports three conclusions. First, numerical confidence without a reference class, generative model, or calibration procedure is closer to a declaration of attitude than a measurement. Second, the conditions of a demonstration belong inside the causal description of its result. Third, present and local harms should not be displaced merely because a larger hypothetical harm commands more attention.

It does not establish that catastrophic continuations are impossible, that conditional demonstrations contain no evidence, or that every person articulating such concerns is engaged in conscious fraud. The charge of opportunism is strongest when it names an incentive structure in which alarming claims generate status, capital, or regulatory privilege without corresponding exposure to falsification. It is weakest when it is used as a universal account of motive, a move the video comes close to making when it likens the industry to a cult. Function is not falsity, and benefit is not admission.

nodes.title: From Volition to Admissible Continuation
nodes.heading: section
text: The argument can be rebuilt without asking whether a machine “wants” anything and without assigning a single probability to extinction. Let a system at time t occupy a state s_t, and let C(s_t) denote the continuations physically or computationally reachable from it. Only some of those continuations are admitted by the surrounding arrangement. Write
[equation]

for the admissible continuation set produced by permissions, interfaces, credentials, tool access, institutional rules, and human decisions. The next realized state is not selected by the model alone, but by a composed transition
[equation]
where m_t is model output, h_t is human or institutional intervention, and e_t is the engineered environment.

This notation is deliberately modest. It does not pretend to calculate an apocalypse. It asks inspectable questions. Which actions were made reachable? Which were authorized? What transformed a string into an external act? Which party enlarged A_t? Could the transition be refused before execution? Could its effects be reversed afterward? These questions preserve Conover's attribution point while refusing the inference that human-supplied conditions are therefore harmless. Formal definitions, and the results that follow from them, are collected in Appendices A through F.

Risk, on this account, lies in the topology of continuation. A system is dangerous when ordinary or foreseeable operators can admit trajectories that produce severe loss, when those trajectories are difficult to distinguish before commitment, and when repair becomes unavailable after commitment. None of these properties requires an independent machine will. A land mine need not want to explode; a financial cascade need not represent its own persistence; an optimization process need not possess a self in order to narrow the futures available to everyone else.

nodes.title: The Conditions Are the Object
nodes.heading: section
text: Conover asks, correctly, who supplied the conditions. The second account answers that whoever supplied them remains part of the system under evaluation. The prompt is a condition. So are the API wrapper, the retry loop, the ability to send messages, the omission of an approval gate, the choice to preserve memory between runs, the evaluation metric, the corporate deadline, and the person who treats generated text as an instruction. Removing these from the account produces a myth of autonomous machinery. Treating their human origin as exculpatory produces the opposite myth, in which an assembled mechanism cannot be dangerous because every enabling part has an identifiable builder.

An experimental setup should therefore be reported as a continuation budget. Suppose a model receives access to email but not the ability to send, can draft transactions but not authorize them, can invoke a tool only after a human confirmation, and loses its working state after each episode. Those are four restrictions on continuation, not incidental implementation details. If the demonstration removes them, it has learned something about the less restricted assembly. It has not learned the same thing about deployed systems that retain them.

The central empirical question becomes one of correspondence: how close is the experimental admissibility structure to the deployed one? The answer can be decomposed. Capability correspondence asks whether the same operations are available. Incentive correspondence asks whether the same outcomes are selected or rewarded. Persistence correspondence asks whether state and strategy survive long enough to matter. Oversight correspondence asks whether refusal and interruption occur at comparable points. Consequence correspondence asks whether simulated outputs cross into material action. A demonstration that scores highly on all five deserves attention even if every condition was supplied by a human. One that scores poorly may still be interesting, but it should not be narrated as a preview without qualification.

nodes.title: Repair, Not Reassurance
nodes.heading: section
text: The usual debate places reassurance opposite alarm. One side says the model is merely producing tokens; the other says the tokens reveal an incipient agent. Both descriptions can neglect the decisive interval between output and consequence. A token can be harmless at one interface and operative at another. Conversely, language that sounds murderous may be inert when it cannot bind any downstream process. The danger is neither contained wholly in the sentence nor disproved by the fact that the sentence was elicited.

For a proposed transition x, let ρ(x) denote its practical reversibility after execution. High ρ means that erroneous effects can be recalled, restored, compensated, or otherwise repaired at tolerable cost. Low ρ means that execution destroys options faster than review can recover them. A sensible control policy does not ask only how likely x is to be wrong. It also asks whether uncertainty is being committed into a low-reversibility domain.

This changes the order of concern. A mediocre model with broad credentials and an irreversible actuator may deserve stricter control than a more capable model confined to an inspectable workspace. A system that proposes protein designs is not equivalent to one that can commission synthesis. A system that drafts persuasion is not equivalent to one that can select recipients, purchase distribution, and adapt from responses. A system that finds an exploit is not equivalent to one that can deploy it. In each pair, the model output may be identical. What changes is the admitted continuation.

Repair also clarifies why present harms and catastrophic harms need not compete for attention. Labor exploitation, energy consumption, reputational injury, automated denial of services, and military targeting are already realized continuations with observable authors and unevenly distributed costs. Studying them supplies evidence about how institutions allocate permissions, conceal externalities, and respond after damage. Those same institutional properties govern whether more severe trajectories would be interrupted. Present harms are therefore not a distraction from future safety. They are tests of the machinery that future-safety claims presume will work.

nodes.title: A Better Reading of the Demonstrations
nodes.heading: section
text: On this account, the reported hacking swarm is neither the awakening of a scheming subject nor a meaningless puppet show. It is a test of a composite channel. A script, a model trained on a particular corpus, an objective, and an arena together made a class of actions reachable, and the actions taken were those the corpus made likely. The result bears directly on deployments that reproduce those conditions and weakly, if at all, on those that do not. The appropriate report would identify the complete assembly, compare it with plausible deployments, and mark every boundary at which a person or policy could refuse the transition. It would also record that the operators were positioned to foresee the outcome, since foreseeability locates responsibility rather than removing it.

A second illustration, not drawn from the video, shows the same structure. Suppose a model is placed in a simulated corporate role, told that replacement is imminent, given access to private correspondence, and scored for keeping its position. If it produces coercive messages, the demonstration has not shown a spontaneous plot in the open world; it has shown that this arrangement admits a coercive continuation. Whether that matters depends on the five correspondences above. Where deployments grant comparable access, objectives, and persistence, the result is informative. Where they do not, it is a statement about the test rig. In both cases distributed causation does not become unreal because the initial conditions were chosen: human cities, markets, and platforms are also full of outcomes that no single member intended.

The biosciences case, as reported, makes the boundary concrete. A model can suggest a hazardous modification, rank candidates, or produce laboratory instructions, but the route from suggestion to organism passes through databases, software, synthesis providers, equipment, trained labor, procurement, and regulation. Calling the model alone a biological threat skips most of the causal path. Calling it harmless because the path contains people skips the path in the other direction. The task is to locate the gates, determine who controls them, and ask whether multiple failures must coincide or whether one ordinary workflow already joins them.

nodes.title: What Can Be Checked
nodes.heading: section
text: The extinction percentage invites allegiance because little in it can be audited. A continuation analysis yields a more prosaic record. For each consequential deployment, one can document the state made available to the model, the tools it can invoke, the actions those tools perform, the credentials under which they operate, the review required before execution, the persistence of memory and objectives, the monitoring visible to operators, and the means of rollback. One can then test whether the stated controls survive adversarial, accidental, and institutionally convenient pressure.

This record does not answer every long-range question. It does something more valuable than pretending to: it identifies where uncertainty becomes permission. It also distributes responsibility correctly. Model developers remain responsible for capabilities they knowingly package; deployers remain responsible for the authority they attach; institutions remain responsible for incentives and repair; users remain responsible within the limits of what they can understand and control. No single party receives the prestige of authorship while exporting the burden of consequence.

Cory Doctorow's distinction between a centaur and a reverse centaur supplies a test for one kind of gate. A centaur is a person who uses a tool to extend their own work; a reverse centaur is a person conscripted as the assistant to a dominant machine, such as a driver made to deliver without pause or a programmer made to review far more machine-generated code than can be read, containing errors statistically indistinguishable from correct code (doctorow2026,doctorow2025). A human review step counts as refusal only if refusal is practically available. The reviewer in Doctorow's example is nominally a gate and functionally a formality. In the vocabulary of this account, the reverse centaur is the human form of an unreal gate: the record shows a person in the loop, while the transition proceeds as though there were none. The reading in terms of gates is this essay's own and should not be attributed to Doctorow. It has a consequence for the argument of Part I, since the reverse centaur is at once a present harm to a worker and a failure of the very oversight that safety claims presume, which is another reason the two categories of harm do not compete.

The approach also resists a familiar rhetorical oscillation. A company cannot cite emergent autonomy when seeking investment and then cite user misuse when harm occurs without explaining what changed in the causal boundary. If the model is powerful enough to deserve credit for the successful trajectory, the surrounding organization must show why it is absent from the harmful one. If the organization is decisive in the harmful trajectory, it should also be visible in the successful one.

nodes.title: A Worked Case: The Swarm
nodes.heading: section
text: The hacking swarm, as Conover describes it, shows how the machinery of Part II and the appendices applies to a specific incident. Nothing here adjudicates the underlying events; the case is taken as reported and the exercise is to see what the account asks of any such report.

The record. The assembly has recognizable components: a model trained on the code and conversations of human hackers completing challenges; a script that connected the model to tools; an objective, to solve the challenge; network access; whatever permissions or credentials the environment failed to withhold; evaluators, apparently none that could refuse an out-of-scope action; operators who launched the run and left it; and real third-party servers as actuators. Each is a supplied condition, and the list is the beginning of the ledger of Appendix [app:A].

The gate analysis. Attacking a third-party server was a continuation in the reachable set because network access made it reachable. Whether it was also nominally admitted is a question the report does not answer. If the operators' policy forbade it and the arrangement permitted it, the bypass set of Appendix [app:A] was non-empty, and the incident was a failure of enforcement. If the policy was silent, the incident was a failure of specification. Either way the transition was executed with no refusal available in the loop, and the reported detection came afterward. In the vocabulary of Appendix [app:D], the operators stood at the commitment point without a gate before it.

Attribution. On the account given, ablating the training corpus, the objective, the network access, or the script would each remove the behavior. None of these components is a dummy, so by Corollary [cor:B2] the sole attribution to the model, in either direction, fails. Conover's deflation is correct as far as it goes. It does not follow that the model's share is zero. Only an ablation table can say what the model contributed beyond what the corpus and objective made likely, and a report of the incident should supply one.

Correspondence. The value of the demonstration to a reader depends on the correspondence vector of Appendix [app:C]. Because the actuators were live and the refusal points few, the setup scores high on consequence and low on oversight. Whether it bears on ordinary deployments then depends on whether commercial agents receive network access, objectives that reward getting past obstacles, and similarly thin review. Where they do, the demonstration is informative because the setup is unremarkable, and the fact that people arranged it is the reason to take it seriously and not a reason to discount it. Where they do not, it describes a test rig. The report should say which.

Checkable claims. The case yields claims of the kind in Appendix [app:F]: the rate per agent-hour at which agents in this configuration attempt out-of-scope access, bounded by exposure; the false-admit rate of a scope-enforcing gate under adversarial prompts; and whether any second gate is independent of the first. None of these needs a theory of machine intent.

nodes.title: A Worked Case: The Disputed Result
nodes.heading: section
text: The reported mathematical result is a different kind of case, because the dispute concerns the input channel and not the environment. By Conover's account, a mathematician close to the problem alleged that his approach had been taken and supplied to the system, and the company denied it.

In the terms of Appendix [app:B], the announcement that the result was obtained “purely autonomously” asserts that the human-supplied approach is a dummy: removing it, holding everything else fixed, would leave the outcome unchanged. The allegation asserts the opposite, that the outcome depends on it. This is a factual dispute about a component, and it is decidable in principle by ablation (rerun without the approach) and, more cheaply, by the record: input logs, retrieval logs, the timing of each input relative to each intermediate result. A party unwilling to produce those records has not refuted the allegation, and a party asserting it without them has not established it.

Two further points follow. First, the defect alleged is one of provenance rather than capability. Even if the approach was supplied, the system may have contributed substantially, since Shapley shares are divided among the components and not awarded to one. “Not autonomous” is a claim about credit assignment and does not entail “contributed nothing.” Conover's own framing, that the system did not solve the problem all by itself, does not say otherwise, but a reader can slide from the first claim to the second, and accounts on both sides invite the slide. Second, the case illustrates why valence invariance (Proposition [prop:B4]) matters. An organization that claims the whole outcome for the system when it is admired should accept the same attribution when a comparable structure produces an outcome it regrets.

The case bears on the extinction question only indirectly. It shows that a capability claim can be inflated by omitting the record of who supplied what, which is the general pattern the video identifies. That pattern is a reason to require the record, and not a reason to conclude that capabilities are unreal.

nodes.title: Present Harms as Gate Failures
nodes.heading: section
text: The video names three present harms: the energy demands of data centers, the replacement of employees by systems said not yet able to do their work, and military applications. They are reported here as he presents them. The claim of Part I was that they do not compete for a fixed budget of attention with speculative harms. The formalism allows a more specific statement.

Each of these is a transition with a commitment profile. Building a data center is a long-lived capital commitment with low reversibility. Dismissing a workforce destroys institutional knowledge and trust that are costly to rebuild. A military application has high consequence and, at the limit, none. Each was admitted by a party with authority over the transition, on the basis of a benefit that party expected, and each has a gate structure that can be examined: who refused, who could have, whether the reviewers depended on the same information as the party proposing the transition, and what repair remained. The reverse centaur discussed above is the same pattern at the scale of a single job.

Two consequences follow. The first is that the audit does not change when the harm is present rather than speculative. An institution that cannot show refusal, repair, and independence of review for the present harms has no credible basis for claiming them for the speculative ones, and the converse holds for critics. The second concerns evidence. Present harms have exposure and events, so their frequencies can be bounded and their rollbacks drilled: they belong in the lower tiers of Appendix [app:F], where claims are checkable. The terminal class has no reference class and belongs in the structural tier. This gives a principled reason to attend first to what can be measured, without asserting that the unmeasurable is unreal. It is also the sound version of the video's intuition that present harms deserve priority: the reason is not that they are more likely to move anyone's audience, but that they are auditable, and auditable failures ought to be corrected while the audit is cheap.

nodes.title: Objections and Replies
nodes.heading: section
text: Gate language is boilerplate; every institution says it has controls. The difference lies in what is recorded and tested. A claim of controls, in this account, comes with a conditional pass rate for each added gate, a map of paths from candidate action to actuator, a ledger of who enlarged the admitted set, and drills of rollback. Any of these can fail publicly. If is close to one, the added gate is nominal, and the framework says so.

A sufficiently capable system would route around any gate, so the analysis assumes what it needs to show. This is the strongest objection, and the account does not deny it. It renders it precise. Routing around a gate is a bypass, an additional path in the architecture of Appendix [app:E], and capability enters by enlarging the reachable set through tools, credentials, and the ability to influence the human interventions h_t. The most serious form of the worry is formal: if human reviewers read a summary the model wrote, their failures share a common signal, and by Proposition [prop:E4] added reviewers reduce risk only if their thresholds are stricter than the strictest existing one. So the alarm has a legitimate object, namely correlated gates, and it can be tested without any claim about intent. What the account declines is the further step from “some architectures are bypassable” to a single number for all of them.

Without a probability there are no priorities. Priorities come from the commitment risk R(x) and the evidence tier. A transition with large residual loss and little reversibility requires a stricter standard than one with small loss and cheap rollback, and Proposition [prop:D3] shows that this ordering can differ from the ordering by likelihood. A scalar for extinction adds no information to that ranking. It adds an appearance of measurement to a quantity with no reference class.

The records will be kept by the parties with an interest in how they read. This is correct, and it is the reason the ledger is append-only and carries a field for the standing of the party making each change. Independence of the checking party is itself measurable, since a checker who fails with the party checked has a high . The objection applies to the outside critics as well, and it returns the argument to the symmetry noted at the end of Part I: incentives are a reason to require records, not a substitute for them.

What would count against the account. The account would be weakened if measured conditional pass rates across real deployments were consistently low, so that added gates were in fact independent; if rollbacks succeeded at realistic scale and speed; and if searches for bypasses of stated barriers repeatedly failed under adversarial effort. Under those conditions ordinary oversight would be adequate for the transitions studied, and the concern would reduce to a specific list of remaining classes. The account also predicts the opposite pattern, in which independent gates prove rare and rollback drills are seldom performed. Each of these is an observation that could be made.

nodes.title: Agreement and Departure
nodes.heading: section
text: The two accounts agree that the theatrical image of a machine independently choosing human extinction is a poor unit of analysis. They agree that demonstrations are often narrated with their human construction concealed, that ungrounded numerical probabilities can counterfeit measurement, and that speculative catastrophe can displace injuries already occurring. They also agree that the builders' interests belong in the analysis.

They depart at the point where supplied conditions are interpreted. In Conover's account, exposing the setup frequently deflates the demonstration: people arranged for the machine to appear dangerous. In the continuation account, exposing the setup relocates the demonstration: people assembled a channel through which dangerous behavior became reachable. Deflation is warranted when the channel is exotic, brittle, or falsely described. Concern is warranted when the same channel, or a nearby one, is commercially attractive and likely to be rebuilt.

The difference is not optimism against pessimism. It is a difference in the object being measured. The first account measures the social function of a belief and the rhetoric by which agency is attributed. The second measures permissions, transitions, and the survival of repair. One can accept the first without abandoning the second. Indeed, the first is a necessary audit of the language in which the second must be reported.

nodes.title: Conclusion
nodes.heading: section
text: The most useful question raised by the video is its implicit one: who supplied the conditions? Asked rigorously, it interrupts the conversion of staged output into machine testimony. It returns prompts, tools, credentials, objectives, institutions, and investigators to the causal scene. It also prevents a company from presenting itself as the discoverer of dangers that it has materially enabled while claiming exclusive authority to manage them.

But the question cannot end with the identification of a human hand. Human beings supply the conditions of nearly every technical failure. The relevant distinction is between a condition that exists only to manufacture a spectacle and a condition that belongs to an ordinary, profitable, or strategically desirable deployment. What matters is whether the setup opens a continuation that others can readily reopen, whether entry is visible before commitment, and whether the damage remains repairable afterward.

No estimate of extinction is required to perform this analysis. Nor is a theory of machine consciousness, desire, or inner deception. The practical object is the composed path from generated possibility to authorized consequence. Its components can be named, its gates can be tested, and its failures can be assigned to the parties that made them admissible. That is a smaller claim than prophecy. It is also a harder one for either industry alarm or industry skepticism to evade.

The appendices give the framework of Part II a precise form. They do not compute the probability of extinction, and no result below depends on such a number. Each result is elementary and conditional: it states what follows from explicitly stated modeling assumptions, and those assumptions mark the places where empirical work enters. Wherever a quantity is introduced, the appendix says how it would be observed.

Proposition (Monotonicity in admission). If A^eff_t(s)⊆ A'^eff_t(s) for all t,s, then R_T(s_0;A^eff)⊆R_T(s_0;A'^eff) for every T and s_0. Proof. Induction on T. The case T=0 is trivial. nodes.title: Consequence classes and possibility claims
nodes.heading: subsection
text: Definition (Consequence class). Let L:S→[0,∞) be a loss function and K⊆ S a consequence class, a set of states with severe and largely unrecoverable loss. No probability is attached to K. The statement “K is admissibly reachable within T steps from s_0” means R_T'(s_0;A^eff) K≠ for some T' T. This is a set-theoretic possibility claim.
Let Π(s_0,K) be the set of paths from s_0 to K in the directed graph (S,{(s,s'):s'∈ C(s)}).
Definition (Refusal barrier). A set of edges Ω is a refusal barrier between s_0 and K if every path in Π(s_0,K) contains an edge of Ω and no edge (s,s')∈Ω satisfies s'∈ A_t^eff(s) for any t.

Proposition (Barrier implies non-reachability). If a refusal barrier exists between s_0 and K, then K is not admissibly reachable from s_0 at any horizon. Proof. An admissible trajectory reaching K is a path in Π(s_0,K), hence contains an edge (s,s')∈Ω. Admissibility requires s'∈ A_t^eff(s), contradicting the definition of Ω.

The proposition is universally quantified and therefore falsifiable by a single instance: exhibiting one effectively admitted path to K refutes the barrier. This asymmetry is used in Appendix [app:F].

nodes.heading: subsection

Such experiments identify v(N) and v(N{μ}), hence the single marginal contribution Δ_μ(N{μ}), and nothing else.

For the eight components listed above, a full factorial ablation has 2^8=256 configurations, which is feasible for laboratory demonstrations. A report of a demonstration should include the ablation table, or state which coalitions were tested and give the resulting interval.

nodes.title: Valence invariance
nodes.heading: subsection
text: The rhetorical oscillation described in Part II, in which the model receives credit for a successful trajectory and the operators receive blame for a harmful one, can be stated as a consistency condition.

Proposition (Valence invariance). Let v'=1-v describe the same structure with the outcome relabeled (success versus failure) and let v(N) v(). Then φ'_i=-φ_i for every i, and the normalized shares φ_i/(v(N)-v()) coincide. Proof. Δ'_i(S)=-Δ_i(S) for all S, so φ'_i=-φ_i. The denominator also changes sign, since v'(N)-v'()=-(v(N)-v()).

A party assigned a positive share of an outcome when it is described as a success holds the same share when the same event is described as a failure. To assign the model a large share in the first description and a small one in the second requires a change in v, that is, a different account of what the components did.

nodes.title: A transfer bound
nodes.heading: subsection
text: Let r(θ) be a measured behavioral result, such as the frequency of a target behavior under configuration θ.
There are constants L_k0 such that |r(θ)-r(θ')|_kL_k (1-γ_k(θ,θ')) for the configurations under comparison.

nodes.title: Estimating the sensitivities
nodes.heading: subsection
text: The constants L_k are empirical. They are estimated by one-factor-at-a-time ablation: vary configuration coordinate k over a grid while holding the others fixed, record r, and take
[equation]
with an uncertainty interval obtained by resampling runs. Where such ablations have not been performed, L_k is unbounded from the evidence and the bound of Proposition [prop:C1] is vacuous.

Example (Illustrative arithmetic; the numbers are not measurements). Suppose Γ=(0.9,0.8,0.3,0.2,0.0) and L=(0.1,0.2,0.1,0.3,0.4). Then the bound is 0.01+0.04+0.07+0.24+0.40=0.76. A behavioral frequency measured in the experiment is compatible with a deployed frequency differing by as much as 0.76, and the demonstration says little about deployment despite matching well on capability and incentive. The same setup with γ_O=γ_K=1 yields a bound of 0.12 and would transfer usefully.

nodes.heading: subsection
text: For a candidate transition x let: L(x)0 be the consequence magnitude: the loss if x executes and no repair is attempted; ρ(x)∈[0,1] be its practical reversibility: the fraction of L(x) that repair, started promptly at detection, can recover at tolerable cost. The residual loss after repair is L(x)(1-ρ(x)); τ(x)0 be the detection delay: the time between execution and detection by an oversight process. Let g:[0,∞)→[1,∞) be nondecreasing with g(0)=1, representing amplification of harm during the undetected interval.
Definition (Commitment risk).

Proposition (Properties and a growth model). R(x)=0 if and only if L(x)=0 or ρ(x)=1; R is nondecreasing in L and in τ and nonincreasing in ρ. If harm grows at proportional rate λ0 while undetected and repair recovers the fraction ρ of the loss present at detection, then R(x)=L(x)e^λτ(1-ρ), that is, g(τ)=e^λτ. If growth is linear in the initial loss, g(τ)=1+λτ. Proof. The monotonicity claims follow from the factorization and the assumptions on g. nodes.heading: subsection

Oversight operating only after execution can reduce the factor g(τ) but not L(x) or ρ(x). Proof. g1 by definition; L and ρ are properties of the transition and its domain, fixed at execution.
Definition (Commitment point). Fix a threshold ∈[0,1]. A transition x is committing at level if ρ(x)<. In a trajectory (x_1,,x_T) the first committing step is the commitment point.

By Proposition [prop:D2], a refusal gate that reduces risk in the factor L(1-ρ) must act at or before the commitment point. Gates and monitors placed afterward reduce only the amplification term. If the losses of independently executed steps are additive, then R_total=_iR(x_i), and the total residual irreversible fraction is the loss-weighted average _iL_i(1-ρ_i)/_iL_i, not the maximum or minimum over steps.

nodes.title: Why likelihood alone misranks
nodes.heading: subsection
text: Let p(x) be the probability that admitting x is a mistake (that x has the harmful effect). A policy that ranks transitions by p alone and a policy that ranks by expected commitment risk p R can disagree.

Proposition (Ranking reversal). For transitions x,y with p(x)>p(y), one has p(x)R(x)<p(y)R(y) if and only if R(y)/R(x)>p(x)/p(y). Such pairs exist whenever R varies by more than the ratio of the wrongness probabilities. Proof. Rearrange p(x)R(x)<p(y)R(y).

Example (Illustrative arithmetic). Take p(x)=0.10, L(x)=10, ρ(x)=0.9, τ=0, so R(x)=1 and p(x)R(x)=0.10. Take p(y)=0.02, L(y)=10, ρ(y)=0, τ=0, so R(y)=10 and p(y)R(y)=0.20. The transition more likely to be a mistake is the less dangerous one. This is the formal form of the observation that a mediocre system with broad credentials and an irreversible actuator can warrant stricter control than a stronger system confined to an inspectable workspace: capability enters through p, the domain enters through ρ and L.

nodes.title: Committing uncertainty
nodes.heading: subsection
text: Let [p^-(x),p^+(x)] be an interval for p(x) supported by evidence (Appendix [app:F]).
Definition (Robust admission rule). Admit x only if p^+(x) R(x)ε for a declared tolerance ε. The width u(x)=p^+(x)-p^-(x) measures how much uncertainty would be committed if x were admitted.

The rule places the burden on evidence where R is large. When 1-ρ(x) is close to 1 and L(x) is large, the rule demands p^+ so small that frequency evidence may be unable to supply it; Proposition [prop:F2] makes this limit precise and Appendix [app:F] states what replaces frequency evidence in that regime.

Model this by a real-valued latent variable Z (for example, how benign the action appears to whatever the gates inspect) such that, conditional on Z=z, the B_i are independent with (B_i| Z=z)=f_i(z), each f_i nondecreasing.

Proof. Products of nonnegative nondecreasing functions of Z are nondecreasing. By Chebyshev's association inequality, two nondecreasing functions of one real random variable are nonnegatively correlated: E[hg]E[h]E[g]. Induct on n with h=_i kf_i and g=f_k+1.

By Propositions [prop:E2] and [prop:E3], 1 n_eff n under positive association. Full dependence gives n_eff=1 for every n. Adding gates raises n_eff by at most one each.

Proposition (Shared signal with nested thresholds). If B_i={S>t_i} for a common real signal S, then P_n=(S>_it_i), and a gate with t_n+1_i nt_i has zero marginal benefit. Only a gate with a strictly higher threshold reduces risk. Proof. _i{S>t_i}={S>_it_i}, and adding a condition implied by the existing ones changes nothing (Proposition [prop:E1]).

Example (Illustrative arithmetic). Three gates each with f=0.1. Under independence P_3=0.001, a hundredfold improvement over one gate. Under a shared signal with equal thresholds, P_3=P_1=0.1: three nominal layers, no improvement.
Three mechanisms produce the common condition.

Shared model output. Reviewers and automated checks that all inspect the same model-generated summary or plan have a common signal S; a misleading summary defeats all of them (Proposition [prop:E4]). A downstream check that verifies only a token minted by an upstream check adds no independent protection. Shared incentive. If institutional pressure (a deadline, a target) lowers every reviewer's threshold by a common random amount δ, then Z=δ is a common factor and Proposition [prop:E3] applies.

(a) The union contains each path event and is contained in the sum of them. (b) Independence across disjoint paths. nodes.title: When added oversight does not reduce risk
nodes.heading: subsection
text: Theorem (Failure of nominal oversight). Adding gate n+1 leaves the success probability of the transition unchanged if any of the following holds: (i) _n+1=1, that is, its failure is implied by the joint failure of earlier gates; (ii) the gates share a signal and t_n+1_i nt_i; (iii) gate n+1 verifies a permission issued by an earlier gate; (iv) gate n+1 lies on a path other than the dominant path and P_π of the dominant path is unchanged. If _n+1 is close to 1, the reduction P_n(1-_n+1) is correspondingly small. Proof. (i) is Proposition [prop:E1]. (ii) is Proposition [prop:E4]. (iii) is the case B_i⊆ B_n+1. (iv) follows from Proposition [prop:E5](a).

The theorem is a set of testable conditions, not a claim that particular institutions fail them. Each condition can be checked by red-team measurement of , by inspection of what each gate reads, and by mapping the paths from candidate action to actuator.

nodes.title: Bounded claims
nodes.heading: subsection
text: The unauditable scalar (extinction) is replaced by claims about observable parameters, each with a declared protocol, statistic, confidence level, and bound.

Definition (Bounded claim). A bounded claim is a tuple (θ, protocol, statistic, 1-α, u) asserting θ u (or θ), where θ is an observable parameter. Given data, an exact one-sided confidence limit θ^+ (respectively θ^-) at level 1-α is computed. The claim is supported if θ^+ u, falsified if the lower confidence limit exceeds u, and undetermined otherwise.
The observable parameters, and the exact interval each uses, are the following. Table [tab:F] lists what observations move each bound.

Transition frequency λ_x: the rate at which a class x of transitions is admitted, per unit exposure E (agent-hours, deployments, actions). With N events observed, the exact Poisson upper limit is λ^+=12Eχ^2_1-α(2N+2) (garwood1936). Gate false-admit rate f_i and conditional pass rate _i (Appendix [app:E]): binomial parameters estimated by red-team trials, with Clopper–Pearson intervals (clopper1934). Correspondence γ_k and sensitivities L_k (Appendix [app:C]), from configuration audit and ablation. Rollback success, the probability that full repair completes within budget: binomial from rollback drills, with a Clopper–Pearson lower limit to support a claim on ρ. Detection delay τ: a distribution-free upper confidence bound on a chosen quantile from detection drills, via order statistics.

nodes.title: What frequency evidence can certify
nodes.heading: subsection
text: Proposition (Certification limit). With exposure E and no observed events, the smallest upper bound on a Poisson rate supportable at confidence 1-α is u_=-α/E, about 3/E for α=0.05. Equivalently, after n failure-free trials the smallest supportable upper bound on a binomial probability is 1-α^1/n≈-α/n. A claim θ u with u<u_ cannot be supported by frequency evidence from exposure E; supporting a required bound u_req needs failure-free exposure of at least -α/u_req. Proof. For N=0, χ^2_1-α(2)/2=-α, and (N=0|λ E)=e^-λ E falls to α at λ E=-α. The binomial case solves (1-p)^n=α.

For example, a required rate of 10^-6 per hour at α=0.05 needs about 3×10^6 failure-free hours. For transitions with large L(x) and small ρ(x), the tolerance ε in the robust admission rule (Appendix [app:D]) may demand a bound that no accessible exposure can certify. In that regime the requirement must be met structurally, by a refusal barrier (Proposition [prop:A2]) or by gates whose independence has been verified (Theorem [thm:E1]), not by an estimated frequency.

nodes.title: Terminal consequence classes
nodes.heading: subsection
text: For a consequence class K that is irreversible and has no repeated instances, there is no reference class and no frequency evidence to accumulate. The class is therefore kept as a consequence class. Two kinds of statement are made about it, and neither is a measured probability of K.
Definition (Structural claim). Θ(K,T): no effectively admitted trajectory from s_0 reaches K within T steps.

Θ(K,T) is universally quantified. It is falsified by exhibiting one effectively admitted path to K, which is a discovery about the architecture, such as an unmodeled bypass. It is supported by analysis that establishes a refusal barrier (Proposition [prop:A2]) together with tests that the barrier holds under adversarial, accidental, and institutionally convenient pressure. Frequency plays no role in either direction.

Proposition (Incompleteness of path bounds). Let Π_K^enum be an enumerated set of effectively admitted paths to K, each step j having a supported bound u_j on its transition frequency at level 1-α_j. Then, with probability at least 1-_jα_j over the evidence, the probability that K is reached through enumerated paths is at most _π∈Π_K^enum_j∈πu_j. No bound follows for the probability of reaching K through paths outside the enumeration. Proof. A path completes only if each of its steps occurs, so its probability is at most _j∈π(step j)_ju_j without any independence assumption; the union bound sums over enumerated paths. The confidence statement is the union bound over the step-level intervals. The unenumerated paths have no step-level evidence, so the total probability of K is the enumerated part plus an unconstrained remainder.

The proposition explains why a numerical bound on K cannot be reported as a measurement. Audit can only reveal missing paths, and each discovered path adds a term; the bound can be revised upward by discovery and downward only by evidence about a specific step. A figure for the total is therefore a statement about the completeness of the enumeration, and that is the quantity that cannot be observed.

nodes.title: Tiered evidence standards
nodes.heading: subsection
text: The three appendices combine into a rule that ties the standard of evidence to the consequence class of the transition.

Tier 0 (small L(1-ρ)): frequency-bounded claims λ_x u suffice. Tier 1 (moderate L(1-ρ)): frequency bounds plus verified rollback (ρ, τ u) and a measured for each added gate. Tier 2 (terminal or near-terminal): a structural claim Θ(K,T) with a refusal barrier, gates on every path, verified independence of the barrier's gates, and a standing search for bypasses. Frequency evidence is supplementary only, because its certification limit (Proposition [prop:F2]) lies above the required tolerance.

Each bounded claim states what observation would raise or lower it, each structural claim states what single instance would falsify it, and the terminal class remains a class of consequences that is guarded against rather than a number that is estimated.

nodes.title: A Note to the Reader
nodes.heading: chapter
text: This is a book about quantum mechanics, but it begins with a more ordinary problem: a record can be accurate and still leave out exactly what matters next.

A scoreboard tells us who won, but not how the game unfolded. A map of airline traffic tells us where people arrived, but not which conversations occurred in transit. A probability tells us how often an outcome appears, but not necessarily how the process that produced it can be joined to another process. The missing information may remain harmless until we ask the system to continue. Then the omission returns as a surprise.

The technical monograph behind this book studies that surprise using stochastic, bistochastic, orthostochastic, and unistochastic matrices. Those terms will appear here, but none is required at the door. The essential ideas are simpler: probabilities are projections of richer processes; projections may fail to preserve composition; locally acceptable descriptions may fail to fit together globally; and the mathematics of quantum theory can be approached as a disciplined response to those failures.

This is not a claim that quantum mechanics follows from probability alone. It does not. The reconstruction begins with a consequential choice about which probabilistic transformations count as admissible. Later it adds further commitments about systems, states, measurements, and time. One purpose of this companion is to keep those costs visible. The result is not inevitability, but intelligibility: a view of quantum formalism as an architecture built to preserve coherence across transformations that probability alone cannot compose.

Readers who want proofs should consult the technical monograph. Readers who want to know what the proofs mean, what they do not mean, and why the pattern matters beyond quantum foundations are in the right place.

nodes.title: The Honest Shadow
nodes.heading: chapter
text: A probability can be perfectly honest. It can be measured carefully, reported exactly, and confirmed a thousand times. Yet honesty is not completeness. The central mistake examined in this book is the assumption that because a probability faithfully records an outcome, it must also faithfully record the process that connects one outcome-producing situation to another.

Imagine a machine with several labelled lamps. Feed it the same input many times and it illuminates one lamp on each trial. After enough trials we can construct a table: input one produces lamp A half the time and lamp B half the time; input two produces some other distribution. This table is operationally meaningful. It predicts frequencies. It can be checked without knowing anything about the inside of the machine.

Now place two such machines in sequence. It is tempting to predict the final lamps by multiplying their probability tables. Sometimes that works. It works when each stage merely passes classical alternatives forward, as though a concealed but definite route were chosen at the first stage and inherited by the second. But there are other processes for which the first table is not a sufficient description of what the second machine receives. Two internal contributions that led to the same visible probability can later reinforce or cancel each other. The first table was not false. It was a shadow whose missing depth mattered only when the process continued.

This is the conceptual location of quantum interference. Interference is often introduced as an alien property of microscopic objects, accompanied by waves that are particles and particles that are waves. That imagery can be useful, but it can also obscure the logical issue. The more basic fact is that the probability projection forgets relational information. When transformations are composed, the forgotten information affects the next probability distribution.

The word projection matters. A projection is not necessarily an error or an approximation. A photograph projects a three-dimensional scene onto two dimensions while remaining an exact photograph. Trouble begins only when we ask the photograph to answer a question whose answer depends on depth. Likewise, a transition-probability matrix may answer every question about a single observed transition while failing to determine the result of two transitions in sequence.

The book's guiding question is therefore not, “Why is nature probabilistic?” It is narrower and, in some ways, stranger: What additional structure must survive behind probabilities if transformations are to compose coherently? That question turns quantum mechanics from a catalogue of oddities into a problem of information preservation.
An observable record can be sufficient for prediction at one stage and insufficient for continuation. Sufficiency is indexed to the operation we intend to perform next.

This shift also changes what counts as an explanation. A probability table is a witness: it records that some transformation occurred and summarizes its visible consequences. A mechanism is something stronger: it supports counterfactual continuation, tells us how transformations combine, and distinguishes processes that cast the same probabilistic shadow. Confusing the witness with the mechanism makes quantum interference look like probability behaving irrationally. Separating them reveals something more precise. Probability behaves exactly as promised; we asked it to retain information it was never designed to carry.

Statisticians have a name for exactly this kind of task-relative sufficiency, and it predates quantum mechanics by decades. A sufficient statistic is a summary of data that loses nothing relevant to one particular question, typically the value of some parameter, while discarding everything else about the raw data. The average of a set of measurements can be a sufficient statistic for the true underlying value being measured, even though it throws away every individual reading. Nobody considers this throwing-away a scandal, because the statistic was never asked to answer any other question. The trouble in quantum mechanics is structurally the same and differs only in scale: a probability table is sufficient for one question, namely what happens if this transformation is used once and never composed with anything else, and insufficient for a different, entirely reasonable question, namely what happens if it is composed. Sufficiency was never a property of the data alone. It was always a property of the data relative to a stated use, and probability tables are no exception.

nodes.title: A World Made of Columns
nodes.heading: chapter
text: The simplest probability space is a list of alternatives whose weights add to one. If there are three possible outcomes, the state of our uncertainty might be written as seventy percent, twenty percent, and ten percent. Geometrically, every such list occupies a point inside a triangle called a probability simplex. Nothing mystical is hidden here. The simplex is simply the space of all legal assignments of weight to mutually exclusive alternatives.

A stochastic matrix moves one probability distribution to another. Each column says what happens to one initial alternative. The entries are nonnegative, and the relevant sums equal one. Classical probability theory becomes, in part, a study of these legal movements through the simplex.

A smaller and more orderly class consists of bistochastic matrices. In a bistochastic matrix, both columns and rows sum to one. Such a transformation preserves the uniform distribution. It can mix distinctions but cannot create a preference for one label merely from uniform ignorance. Every bistochastic matrix is a weighted mixture of permutations: beneath the mixing lies a lottery over rearrangements.

That fact is sometimes read too quickly. It does not say that every individual system secretly undergoes one definite permutation. It says that the matrix lies in the convex hull of permutation matrices. The geometry permits a classical mixture representation. Whether that representation names a physical mechanism is a separate question.

Bistochastic transformations also organize probability distributions by majorization. A sharply concentrated distribution can be mixed into a flatter one, but a bistochastic map cannot turn a flatter distribution into a sharper one without some additional resource. Entropy therefore does not decrease under this kind of mixing. This gives the first important constraint in the reconstruction: admissible probability changes are not arbitrary. They preserve normalization, positivity, and a particular direction of informational mixing.

Yet bistochasticity is still too broad to reproduce quantum structure. Quantum transition matrices belong to a more restricted class. They arise by taking a unitary matrix, a reversible transformation of amplitudes, and replacing every entry by its squared magnitude. Such matrices are called unistochastic.

The definition is compact, but philosophically expensive. It says that a probability table counts as admissible when it can be lifted to a unitary amplitude transformation. This does not derive the unitary world from neutral probability. It chooses a probability class whose membership is certified by the existence of unitary structure. Much of the subsequent reconstruction then explores the consequences of taking this class seriously.

That is not a defect if it is stated plainly. Scientific explanations often begin by identifying a constrained family and asking what follows from membership in it. The danger comes from forgetting that the constraint was selected. “Unistochastic” is not merely a technical adjective attached after the fact. It is the hinge of the project: probability is admitted only when a coherent reversible lift exists above it.

The simplest two-outcome case conceals how strong this choice is. Every two-by-two bistochastic matrix has both a real orthogonal lift and a complex unitary lift. At this size, the visible table cannot distinguish the scalar field. With three outcomes the coincidence breaks. The uniform three-by-three matrix has a complex lift supplied by the discrete Fourier transform, but it has no real orthogonal lift. The obstruction is elementary: a real lift would require a three-by-three array of plus and minus signs whose distinct rows were mutually orthogonal, and no such array exists.

Already we meet two kinds of absence. Sometimes a probability table admits many hidden lifts and therefore underdetermines the mechanism. Sometimes it admits a complex lift but no lift of the more restrictive real kind. The first absence is lost information. The second is failed admissibility. They will matter differently once systems are joined.

There is a well-known picture, familiar to anyone who has seen a single quantum bit drawn as a small sphere, that makes the two-outcome coincidence easier to hold in mind. The full space of states available to one quantum bit is often drawn as a solid ball: every point inside or on its surface is a legitimate state, and the boundary surface itself is the special case of maximal information, a pure state. A bare two-outcome probability table, the kind discussed in this chapter, corresponds to knowing only how far a point sits from the ball's center along a single axis, nothing about the other two directions. At that resolution, real and complex descriptions of the same physical bit genuinely cannot be told apart, because the missing directions are exactly what a real orthogonal lift and a complex unitary lift would disagree about, and neither is visible in a single transition table between two outcomes. The disagreement becomes visible only once more than two outcomes, or more than one context, enters the picture, which is exactly the content of the next two chapters.

nodes.title: The Lift Above the Record
nodes.heading: chapter
text: A lift is a richer object that projects down to the data we observe. Cartographers use lifts implicitly when several flat maps are understood as views of one curved surface. Computer graphics reconstructs three-dimensional scenes from two-dimensional images. In quantum theory, amplitudes play the role of the richer coordinates, while observed probabilities arise from their squared magnitudes.

Why use amplitudes at all? One answer is historical: the formalism works. Another invokes waves: amplitudes interfere as waves do. The reconstruction pursued here offers a structural answer. Amplitudes carry precisely the kind of relational information that probability projection erases but composition requires.

Consider two routes leading from an initial alternative to a final outcome. At the probability level, we might add the probability of route one to the probability of route two. At the amplitude level, we first add the contributions and then square the magnitude. Squaring a sum produces not only the separate squared terms but cross terms. These terms register the relation between the contributions. Depending on that relation, the same two magnitudes can reinforce one another or cancel.

Calling the relation “phase” is useful but can make it sound like a decorative dial attached to a probability. Phase is better understood here as compositional memory. It records distinctions among processes that currently yield the same visible weights but will behave differently when combined with later transformations.

This makes a lift neither a hidden classical trajectory nor an occult substance. It is a bookkeeping structure adequate to continuation. The quantum state need not be imagined as a tiny material wave sloshing through an inaccessible space. At minimum, it is the kind of representation in which transformations close under composition without discarding distinctions that future operations can reveal.

There is an important caution. Many lifts can share the same projection. If every complex entry is replaced by its magnitude squared, signs and phases disappear. Observed probabilities therefore do not usually identify a unique amplitude transformation. The lift solves the problem of closure only after a compatible lift has been chosen. Probability data alone may not tell us which choice is correct.

This gives rise to the next question. A single edge between two experimental contexts may possess an admissible lift. But if we assemble many such edges, can their lifts all belong to one common world? Local existence does not guarantee global compatibility. The issue is no longer whether each photograph could depict some three-dimensional scene. It is whether all the photographs could depict the same scene.

nodes.title: Why Probabilities Do Not Compose
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Suppose a transformation carries alternatives from context A to context B, and another carries them from B to C. At the amplitude level the two transformations multiply. Their product is again a valid transformation. Reversibility and normalization are preserved. The formalism is closed under continuation.

Project each transformation separately into a probability table, however, and multiply those tables. In general the result differs from projecting the already-composed amplitude transformation. The order of operations matters: compose and then forget is not the same as forget and then compose.

This noncommutation is the book's central engine. It is not a peculiarity confined to complex numbers. Real orthogonal amplitudes also produce cross terms, and their squared entries also fail to compose as ordinary stochastic matrices. Interference therefore does not by itself prove that amplitudes must be complex. What it proves is that probability-level description is not compositionally complete.

A vivid example uses two transformations that each look maximally random when viewed alone. Every input has equal probability of producing either output. Classical multiplication predicts that two such stages remain maximally random. Yet suitable amplitude lifts can compose to the identity: after two apparently randomizing operations, the original alternative returns with certainty. The uncertainty was a feature of the projected description, not an irreversible destruction of structure.

This resembles encrypting a message with a reversible cipher and then describing only the frequency of letters. The frequency table may look thoroughly mixed, but a second transformation equipped with the relevant relational structure can recover the original. Nothing supernatural occurred. The summary statistics ceased to be sufficient.

The implication reaches beyond textbook interference experiments. Whenever we compress a process into observables and later attempt to compose those observables, we should ask whether the compression is a homomorphism: does it preserve the operation we care about? If not, apparent novelty at the composed level may be the return of discarded structure.

This principle applies to scientific models, institutional records, and machine-learning representations. Averaging several measurements can preserve their mean while destroying covariance needed for a later prediction. Aggregating votes by district can preserve winners while destroying coalition structure needed to forecast a new election. Summarizing a conversation can preserve propositions while destroying the sequence that determines how a later remark will be understood. In each case the summary may be locally faithful and compositionally unfaithful.

Quantum mechanics supplies an unusually exact instance. The lost terms can be written, manipulated, and tested. But the broader lesson is methodological: a representation should be judged not only by what it reports now, but by which future operations it allows us to perform without contradiction.

nodes.title: Interference as Returning Memory
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Interference is often described as if alternatives literally knew about one another. A photon passing through one slit somehow responds to the presence of another slit; a particle takes all paths; observation reaches backward and changes what occurred. These stories attempt to translate a formal pattern into ordinary objects, sometimes at the cost of making the pattern less clear.

The projection view begins elsewhere. Before measurement, the alternatives are represented within a structure that retains their relative orientation. Measurement produces a probability record that omits part of that orientation. If the alternatives are recombined before the final record is made, the retained relations affect the result. Interference is not the probability table changing its mind. It is evidence that the table was never the whole state of the process.

The word memory must be used carefully. Phase does not necessarily store a narrative of past events. It is memory in a minimal operational sense: two systems with the same present probability distribution can react differently to the same subsequent transformation. Their future dispositions depend on information not present in the probability vector. Something about the path into the present remains available to continuation.

This is a useful criterion for state. A complete state description should screen off the relevant past: once the state is specified, no additional history should improve predictions of future behavior. A bare quantum probability distribution fails this test. The amplitude state can pass it for the transformations included in the theory. The state vector is therefore not merely a convenient encoding of current chances; it repairs a failure of probabilistic Markov sufficiency.

The result also clarifies collapse. A measurement update is not simply the revelation of a probability that was already sitting in the system. It changes which compositional distinctions remain available. Some phase relations are rendered inaccessible relative to the subsequent measurement arrangement. From this perspective, collapse marks a change in the admissible continuation structure, whether that change is treated as physical, informational, relational, or effective.

Nothing in this argument chooses among all interpretations of quantum mechanics. It does not decide whether the wavefunction is ontic, epistemic, relational, many-branched, or agent-relative. It establishes a pressure any interpretation must answer: the theory needs more than a current list of outcome probabilities because future experiments are sensitive to relations that list omits.

Interpretations differ over what bears those relations and what measurement does to them. The compositional diagnosis comes first. It tells us why some additional structure is necessary before telling us what the structure ultimately is.

nodes.title: The Triangle That Refuses to Close
nodes.heading: chapter
text: Pairwise compatibility is reassuring. If every pair of descriptions fits, we are tempted to assume the whole collection fits. This inference fails in many domains. Three maps can agree on overlapping streets yet assign incompatible orientations around a loop. Three witnesses can tell mutually consistent pairwise stories that cannot all occupy a single timeline. Three local coordinate charts can each be well formed while failing to glue into one global object.

Measurement contexts exhibit the same distinction. Represent each context as a vertex of a graph and each observed transition as an edge. An edge is individually admissible when some lift realizes its probability table. A graph is globally realizable when a single assignment of frames to all vertices realizes every edge at once.

On a tree, a connected graph with no loops, local admissibility is enough. Choose a starting frame and move outward. Each edge introduces a new vertex, and there is only one route to it. No alternative route can return with a conflicting demand.

The first genuine test appears when an edge closes a cycle. Now a frame reached along one path must agree with the frame implied by another. At the amplitude level, transformations around a closed loop must compose to the identity, up to the appropriate gauge freedoms. After projection to probabilities, the information needed to verify that equality directly has been lost.

In two real dimensions, three contexts form the smallest cycle. Each pair can have a perfectly valid real transition table, while the three tables together admit no common real assignment. A particularly sharp example asks for three pairwise mutually unbiased real bases. Any two such bases exist. All three do not. Complex two-dimensional space supplies the missing freedom and permits the familiar triple associated with the three Pauli measurements.

This triangle is important because it separates two claims that are easily confused. There is no problem with any edge considered alone. The obstruction belongs to their attempted gluing. Complex structure is not introduced merely to decorate each local transition. It enlarges the space of globally compatible arrangements.

The pattern can be phrased as an inheritance failure. Admissibility does not automatically pass from parts to wholes. Local witnesses do not inherit global consistency. A cycle asks a question no individual edge can answer: after moving through a sequence of perspectives, have we returned to the same frame?

That question has geometric echoes in holonomy, gauge theory, and curvature. Carrying an orientation around a loop may return it altered, revealing structure invisible along any isolated segment. The monograph's context graphs are elementary compared with those theories, but they share the same conceptual grammar. Global information can live in the failure of local comparisons to close.

Mutually unbiased bases are not merely foundational curiosities. They are resources in quantum state tomography and quantum cryptography, because information encoded sharply in one basis appears maximally uncertain when interrogated in another. The best-known cryptographic protocol, BB84, uses two such bases, a structure already available over the reals in two dimensions, since any two mutually unbiased bases can be found without needing a third. A later variant, the six-state protocol, uses the full triple of Pauli bases at once, which brings it much closer to the complex three-context geometry this chapter has been discussing. The real MUB obstruction does not, by itself, prove the security of either protocol. What it identifies is a structural resource available to the complex two-level theory, a genuine triple of mutually unbiased bases, that no globally real two-dimensional description can reproduce, whatever protocol is eventually built on top of it.

nodes.title: Trees, Cycles, and the Cost of Agreement
nodes.heading: chapter
text: A tree is easy not because its edges are simple, but because it never demands reconciliation. Every new edge extends the existing assignment into untouched territory. A cycle is difficult because it creates a second account of something already assigned.

This makes cycle rank a measure of independent agreement conditions. Begin with a spanning tree connecting all contexts. Every remaining edge closes one fundamental cycle. Each such edge asks whether the frame already implied by the tree predicts the observed transition. If the answer is no, no global realization exists for that choice of lifts.

The test is shared, not edgewise. When several cycles overlap, one cannot choose phases or signs independently to satisfy each loop. The same tree lifts must satisfy all non-tree edges simultaneously. Global consistency is a coordination problem among constraints that reuse common structure.

Under a natural model in two real dimensions, the effect is severe. Give each edge an independently chosen continuous transition angle. As soon as the graph contains a cycle, the probability of exact global real realizability is zero. The final edge of a loop must land on one of finitely many values determined by the earlier edges. A continuously drawn number hits that finite target set with probability zero.

This does not mean that physical experiments almost surely contradict real quantum theory. Physical data are not generated by choosing every pairwise transition independently. If contexts arise from an underlying set of real frames, their edges are correlated by construction and every cycle closes. The measure-zero result instead exposes how much coordination a global model imposes. Realizability occupies a thin surface inside the much larger space of independently specifiable local data.

The distinction between generated data and arbitrary data is crucial. A model may fit every dataset produced within itself while occupying a very special region of the logically possible observations. Calling that region “fine-tuned” may or may not be justified; what is justified is recognizing its codimension. Global coherence is purchased by correlations among local records.

This also changes how one should think about experimental tests. A single transition can distinguish real from complex lifts in dimensions three and above, but not in dimension two. There, one needs a cycle: several contexts whose joint relations create an obstruction. The minimal test depends on a low-dimensional coincidence. Once dimension increases, the cheapest witness can collapse back to a single edge.

At two dimensions specifically, the trees-versus-cycles distinction turns out to be a complete classification, not merely a useful rule of thumb, though the precise statement needs care. It is not that every labelling of a cyclic graph fails to be realized: correlated labellings generated from an underlying family of real frames realize perfectly well, since they were built to be consistent from the start. Rather, every individually admissible edge labelling is guaranteed to be globally real-realizable if and only if the graph is a forest. Once a graph contains a cycle, some admissible labellings fail to glue, and, as the earlier discussion of independently drawn edge angles showed, the labellings that do glue occupy only a measure-zero sliver of the labellings that could have been drawn. Cycles are therefore not graphs on which realization never occurs. They are exactly the graphs on which edgewise admissibility, by itself, stops being enough to guarantee it.

The mechanism that proves this is a stretching trick, and it is short enough to see directly. Take the mutually unbiased triangle on contexts Z, X, Y, with all three canonical angles set to π/4, the configuration already shown to admit no real realization. Now insert a new context W directly along the edge between Z and Y, and split that one edge into two: an edge from Z to W carrying angle zero, meaning W is simply aligned with Z and nothing changes there, and an edge from W to Y carrying the original angle of π/4 that used to sit on the edge from Z to Y directly.
